text: This page contains Wagon specific information, but the default transport in Maven 3.9.0+ is NOT Wagon anymore. Make sure to check the Resolver Transport guide f
body: This page contains Wagon specific information, but the default transport in Maven 3.9.0+ is NOT Wagon anymore. Make sure to check the Resolver Transport guide first, as things have changed. You can use the default wagon implementation for a given protocol, or you can select an alternative wagon provider on a per-protocol basis. For more information, see the Guide to Wagon Providers [3]. The default wagon http(s) is the HttpClient based on Apache Http Client 4.5 . HTTP connection pooling prevents reopening new connections to the same server for each request. This pool feature is configurable with some parameters [4]. The default wagon comes with some default configuration: http(s) connection pool: default to 20. readTimeout: default to 1800000 (~30 minutes) (see section Read time out below) default Preemptive Authentication only with PUT (GET doesn't use anymore default Preemptive Authentication)

page: HTTP options of the Wagon transport
title: Configuring GET, HEAD, PUT, or All of the Above
text: Starting with Maven 3.9.0 native HTTP transport will pick up the "all" settings only (get, head, put are neglected!)" but it will WARN about its deprecation. Fo
body: Starting with Maven 3.9.0 native HTTP transport will pick up the "all" settings only (get, head, put are neglected!)" but it will WARN about its deprecation. For users sticking with Wagon nothing changes. In all of the examples below, it's important to understand that you can configure the HTTP settings for all requests made to a given server, or for only one method. To configure all methods for a server, use the following section of the settings.xml file: <settings> [...] <servers> <server> <id> the-server </id> <configuration> <httpConfiguration> <all> [ Your configuration here. ] </all> </httpConfiguration> </configuration> </server> </servers> </settings> On the other hand, if you can live with the default configuration for most requests — say, HEAD and GET requests, which are used to check for the existence of a file and retrieve a file respectively — maybe you only need to configure the PUT method: <settings> [...] <servers> <server> <id> the-server </id> <configuration> <httpConfiguration> <put> [ Your configuration here. ] </put> </httpConfiguration> </configuration> </server> </servers> </settings> For clarity, the other two sections are <get> for GET requests, and <head> for HEAD requests. I know that's going to be hard to remember...

page: HTTP options of the Wagon transport
title: Fine-Tuning HttpClient Parameters
text: Going beyond the power of HTTP request parameters, HttpClient provides a host of other configuration options. In most cases, you won't need to customize these.
terms: b <value> i l d c <value1> <value2> <value3> sprintf http.authentication.preemptive http.protocol.cookie-policy Path
body: Going beyond the power of HTTP request parameters, HttpClient provides a host of other configuration options. In most cases, you won't need to customize these. But in case you do, Maven provides access to specify your own fine-grained configuration for HttpClient. Again, you can specify these parameter customizations per-method (HEAD, GET, or PUT), or for all methods of interacting with a given server. For a complete list of supported parameters, see the link[2] in Resources section below. Non-String Parameter Values Many of the configuration parameters for HttpClient have simple string values; however, there are important exceptions to this. In some cases, you may need to specify boolean, integer, or long values. In others, you may even need to specify a collection of string values. You can specify these using a simple formatting syntax, as follows: booleans: %b,<value> integer: %i,<value> long: %l,<value> (yes, that's an 'L', not a '1') double: %d,<value> collection of strings: %c,<value1>,<value2>,<value3>,... , which could also be specified as: %c, <value1>, <value2>, <value3>, ... As you may have noticed, this syntax is similar to the format-and-data strategy used by functions like sprintf() in many languages. The syntax has been chosen with this similarity in mind, to make it a little more intuitive to use. Example: Using Preemptive Authentication Using the above syntax, you can configure preemptive authentication for PUT requests using the boolean HttpClient parameter http.authentication.preemptive , like this: <settings> <servers> <server> <id> my-server </id> <configuration> <httpConfiguration> <put> <params> <property> <name> http.authentication.preemptive </name> <value> %b,true </value> </property> </params> </put> </httpConfiguration> </configuration> </server> </servers> </settings> Another option is to make write it like this: <settings> <servers> <server> <id> my-server </id> <configuration> <httpConfiguration> <put> <usePreemptive> true </usePreemptive> </put> </httpConfiguration> </configuration> </server> </servers> </settings> Example: Lifting auth scope restriction for external authentication systems Maven Wagon by default limits supplied credentials to the host:port combination scope, ignoring any other target servers. When the target server delegates authentication to an external system, you need to deliberately lift that scope limitation. Configure your server element to pass authentication to all target servers which challenge the client. +---+ settings servers server id_my-server /id_ configuration basicAuthScope host_ANY /host_ port_ANY /port_ !-- or even 443 to force the use of TLS -- /basicAuthScope httpConfiguration all params property name_http.protocol.cookie-policy /name_ value_standard /value_ /property /params /all /httpConfiguration /configuration /server /servers /settings +---+ Ignoring Cookies Like the example above, telling the HttpClient to ignore cookies for all methods of request is a simple matter of configuring the http.protocol.cookie-policy parameter (it uses a regular string value, so no special syntax is required): <settings> <servers> <server> <id> my-server </id> <configuration> <httpConfiguration> <all> <params> <param> <name> http.protocol.cookie-policy </name> <value> ignore </value> </param> </params> </all> </httpConfiguration> </configuration> </server> </servers> </settings> The configuration above can be useful in cases where the repository is using cookies - like the session cookies that are often mistakenly turned on or left on in appservers - alongside HTTP redirection. In these cases, it becomes far more likely that the cookie issued by the appserver uses a Path that is inconsistent with the one used by the client to access the server. If you have this problem, and know that you don't need to use this session cookie, you can ignore cookies from this server with the above configuration.

page: HTTP options of the Wagon transport
title: Introduction
text: The HttpClient-based HTTP wagon offers more control over the configuration used to access HTTP-based Maven repositories. For starters, you have fine-grained con
body: The HttpClient-based HTTP wagon offers more control over the configuration used to access HTTP-based Maven repositories. For starters, you have fine-grained control over what HTTP headers are used when resolving artifacts. In addition, you can also configure a wide range of parameters to control the behavior of HttpClient itself. Best of all, you have the ability to control these headers and parameters for all requests, or individual request types (GET, HEAD, and PUT).

page: HTTP options of the Wagon transport
title: Support for General-Wagon Configuration Standards
text: It should be noted that configuration options previously available in the HttpClient-driven HTTP wagon are still supported in addition to this new, fine-grained
body: It should be noted that configuration options previously available in the HttpClient-driven HTTP wagon are still supported in addition to this new, fine-grained approach. These include the configuration of HTTP headers and connection timeouts. Let's examine each of these briefly: HTTP Headers In all HTTP Wagon implementations, you can add your own HTTP headers like this: <settings> <servers> <server> <id> my-server </id> <configuration> <httpHeaders> <property> <name> Foo </name> <value> Bar </value> </property> </httpHeaders> </configuration> </server> </servers> </settings> It's important to understand that the above approach doesn't allow you to turn off all of the default HTTP headers; nor does it allow you to specify headers on a per-method basis. However, this configuration remains available in both the lightweight and httpclient-based Wagon implementations. Connection Timeouts All wagon implementations that extend the AbstractWagon class, including those for SCP, HTTP, FTP, and more, allow the configuration of a connection timeout, to allow the user to tell Maven how long to wait before giving up on a connection that has not responded. This option is preserved in the HttpClient-based wagon, but this wagon also provides a fine-grained alternative configuration that can allow you to specify timeouts per-method for a given server. The old configuration option - which is still supported - looks like this: <settings> <servers> <server> <id> my-server </id> <configuration> <timeout> 6000 </timeout> <!-- milliseconds --> </configuration> </server> </servers> </settings> ...while the new configuration option looks more like this: <settings> <servers> <server> <id> my-server </id> <configuration> <httpConfiguration> <put> <connectionTimeout> 10000 </connectionTimeout> <!-- milliseconds --> </put> </httpConfiguration> </configuration> </server> </servers> </settings> If all you need is a per-server timeout configuration, you still have the option to use the old <timeout> parameter. If you need to separate timeout preferences according to HTTP method, you can use one more like that specified directly above. Read time out The default timeout is 30 minutes. If you want to change this value, you can add the following setup in your settings: <settings> <servers> <server> <id> my-server </id> <configuration> <httpConfiguration> <put> <readTimeout> 120000 </readTimeout> <!-- milliseconds --> </put> </httpConfiguration> </configuration> </server> </servers> </settings>

page: HTTP options of the Wagon transport
title: Taking Control of Your HTTP Headers
text: As you may have noticed above, the default HTTP headers do have the potential to cause problems. For instance, some websites set the encoding for downloading GZ
body: As you may have noticed above, the default HTTP headers do have the potential to cause problems. For instance, some websites set the encoding for downloading GZipped files as gzip , in spite of the fact that the HTTP request itself isn't being sent using GZip compression. If the client is using the Accept-Encoding: gzip header, this can result in the client itself decompressing the GZipped file during the transfer and writing the decompressed file to the local disk with the original filename. This can be misleading to say the least, and can use up an inordinate amount of disk space on the local computer. To turn off this default behavior, simply disable the default headers. Then, respecify the other headers that you are still interested in, like this: <settings> [...] <servers> <server> <id> openssl </id> <configuration> <httpConfiguration> <put> <useDefaultHeaders> false </useDefaultHeaders> <headers> <property> <name> Cache-control </name> <value> no-cache </value> </property> <property> <name> Cache-store </name> <value> no-store </value> </property> <property> <name> Pragma </name> <value> no-cache </value> </property> <property> <name> Expires </name> <value> 0 </value> </property> <property> <name> Accept-Encoding </name> <value> * </value> </property> </headers> </put> </httpConfiguration> </configuration> </server> [...] </servers> [...] </settings>

page: HTTP options of the Wagon transport
title: The Basics
text: Without any special configuration, Maven's HTTP wagon uses some default HTTP headers and client parameters when managing artifacts. The default headers are: Cac
body: Without any special configuration, Maven's HTTP wagon uses some default HTTP headers and client parameters when managing artifacts. The default headers are: Cache-control: no-cache Cache-store: no-store Pragma: no-cache Expires: 0 Accept-Encoding: gzip In addition, PUT requests made with the HTTP wagon use the following HttpClient parameter: http.protocol.expect-continue=true From the HttpClient documentation[2], this parameter provides the following functionality: Activates 'Expect: 100-Continue' handshake for the entity enclosing methods. The 'Expect: 100-Continue' handshake allows a client that is sending a request message with a request body to determine if the origin server is willing to accept the request (based on the request headers) before the client sends the request body. The use of the 'Expect: 100-continue' handshake can result in noticeable performance improvement for entity enclosing requests (such as POST and PUT) that require the target server's authentication. 'Expect: 100-continue' handshake should be used with caution, as it may cause problems with HTTP servers and proxies that do not support HTTP/1.1 protocol. Without this setting, PUT requests that require authentication transfer their entire payload to the server before that server issues an authentication challenge. In order to complete the PUT request, the client must then re-send the payload with the proper credentials specified in the HTTP headers. This results in twice the bandwidth usage, and twice the time to transfer each artifact. Another option to avoid this double transfer is what's known as preemptive authentication, which involves sending the authentication headers along with the original PUT request. However, there are a few potential issues with this approach. For one thing, in the event you have an unused <server> entry that specifies an invalid username/password combination, some servers may respond with a 401 Unauthorized even if the server doesn't actually require any authentication for the request. In addition, blindly sending authentication credentials with every request regardless of whether the server has made a challenge can result in a security hole, since the server may not make provisions to secure credentials for paths that don't require authentication. We'll discuss preemptive authentication in another example, below.

title: Alternative Wagon providers
text: By default, Maven uses the java.net.URLConnection ( HttpURLConnection ) classes provided with the JDK to access repositories that use the HTTP/HTTPs protocols.
body: By default, Maven uses the java.net.URLConnection ( HttpURLConnection ) classes provided with the JDK to access repositories that use the HTTP/HTTPs protocols. Unfortunately, since this implementation contains certain bugs, Maven users may find themselves unable to connect to servers that demand some configurations. A couple examples of weird behavior include line-wrapping the Authorization header's Base64 value when passwords are long, and using cached values in preemptive authentication for successive connections to the same server. Maven 2.2.0 attempted to amend this problem by switching over to a Wagon implementation that's based on Apache HttpClient. Unfortunately, it soon became apparent that HttpClient doesn't support NTLM (at least, version 2), which effectively means users behind NTLMv2 proxies cannot use Maven 2.2.0. To hopefully resolve this once and for all, Maven 2.2.1 will contain support for specifying which Wagon provider you want to use for a given protocol during the build. The provider name will then be appended to the protocol using the format <protocol>-<provider> to form the component role-hint for the Wagon. As of Maven 2.2.1, there are two ways to specify which Wagon provider should be used: via the command line, or in the <server> configuration section of the settings.xml .

title: Available Wagon Providers
text: Maven 2.2.1 provides two providers for HTTP/HTTPS Wagons: lightweight and httpclient . If you add a new HTTP Wagon implementation via build extension, you'll ne
body: Maven 2.2.1 provides two providers for HTTP/HTTPS Wagons: lightweight and httpclient . If you add a new HTTP Wagon implementation via build extension, you'll need to make sure the extension binds its Wagon components to role-hints of the form <protocol>-<provider> in order to allow users to specify your alternative Wagon provider. For instance, the HttpClient HTTP Wagon component definition looks like this: <component> <role> org.apache.maven.wagon.Wagon </role> <role-hint> http-httpclient </role-hint> <implementation> org.apache.maven.wagon.providers.http.HttpWagon </implementation> <instantiation-strategy> per-lookup </instantiation-strategy> </component> NOTE: The default provider for HTTP/HTTPS Wagons is lightweight .

title: Command-Line Configuration
text: To specify the Wagon provider from the command line, simply use the -Dmaven.wagon.provider.<protocol>=<provider-name> command-line option, like the following: m
terms: Dmaven.wagon.provider. <protocol> <provider-name> mvn Dmaven.wagon.provider.http httpclient clean install
body: To specify the Wagon provider from the command line, simply use the -Dmaven.wagon.provider.<protocol>=<provider-name> command-line option, like the following: mvn -Dmaven.wagon.provider.http=httpclient clean install This instructs Maven to use the HttpClient-based Wagon implementation for connections to HTTP repositories.

title: settings.xml Configuration
text: To specify which Wagon provider to use for a particular server, modify your settings.xml file to add the <wagonProvider> configuration to your <server> entry, l
body: To specify which Wagon provider to use for a particular server, modify your settings.xml file to add the <wagonProvider> configuration to your <server> entry, like the following: <settings> [...] <servers> <server> <id> central </id> <configuration> <wagonProvider> httpclient </wagonProvider> [...] </configuration> </server>

title: Add your first dependency
text: Find a library on Maven Central, add it to your project's POM, use it in your code and run the program with it.
keywords: library add jar add library central.sonatype.com coordinates Apache Commons Lang commons-lang3 StringUtils classpath NoClassDefFoundError package does not exist transitive dependency
body: In this tutorial you make the program from Create your first project greet someone by name. It uses a library from Maven Central, Apache Commons Lang, to write the name with a capital. You find the library, add it to the project, use it in your code and run the program with it. Start in the my-app directory as you left it at the end of that tutorial.

title: Continue with a plugin
text: Starting the program now takes a classpath with two entries. In Add and configure your first plugin you build one JAR that holds your classes and the library, a
body: Starting the program now takes a classpath with two entries. In Add and configure your first plugin you build one JAR that holds your classes and the library, and runs with java -jar .

title: 1. Find the library on Maven Central
text: Maven downloads libraries from Maven Central, the public repository of Java libraries. Each library has coordinates: a groupId , an artifactId and a version , t
body: Maven downloads libraries from Maven Central, the public repository of Java libraries. Each library has coordinates: a groupId , an artifactId and a version , the same three elements your own pom.xml starts with. Open https://central.sonatype.com and search for commons-lang3 . The page of org.apache.commons:commons-lang3 shows the latest version and, under "Snippets", the <dependency> element to copy for Maven. This tutorial uses version 3.21.0.

title: 2. Add the dependency
text: pom.xml has two <dependencies> elements: one inside <dependencyManagement> and one directly under <project> . Add the library to the one directly under <project
body: pom.xml has two <dependencies> elements: one inside <dependencyManagement> and one directly under <project> . Add the library to the one directly under <project> , above the JUnit dependencies: pom.xml <project ... > ... <dependencies> <dependency> <groupId> org.apache.commons </groupId> <artifactId> commons-lang3 </artifactId> <version> 3.21.0 </version> </dependency> <dependency> <groupId> org.junit.jupiter </groupId> <artifactId> junit-jupiter-api </artifactId> <scope> test </scope> </dependency> ... </dependencies> ... </project> A dependency without a <scope> is available to your code, your tests and the program when it runs. The JUnit dependencies have <scope>test</scope> : they are only there for the tests, and do not end up with your program.

title: 3. Use the library
text: Create a class that builds the greeting. StringUtils.defaultIfBlank from Commons Lang replaces an empty name with world , and StringUtils.capitalize writes the
body: Create a class that builds the greeting. StringUtils.defaultIfBlank from Commons Lang replaces an empty name with world , and StringUtils.capitalize writes the first letter as a capital: src/main/java/com/mycompany/app/Greeter.java package com.mycompany.app ; import org.apache.commons.lang3.StringUtils ; public class Greeter { public String greet ( String name ) { return "Hello, " + StringUtils . capitalize ( StringUtils . defaultIfBlank ( name , "world" )) + "!" ; } } Replace App.java so that it greets the name you give on the command line: src/main/java/com/mycompany/app/App.java package com.mycompany.app ; public class App { public static void main ( String [] args ) { String name = String . join ( " " , args ); System . out . println ( new Greeter (). greet ( name )); } }

title: 4. Build the project
text: In the my-app directory, run: mvn package Maven downloads commons-lang3-3.21.0.jar from Maven Central into your local repository, puts it on the classpath and c
terms: my-app mvn package commons-lang3-3.21.0.jar org.apache.commons.lang3 does not exist <dependencies> <dependencyManagement>
body: In the my-app directory, run: mvn package Maven downloads commons-lang3-3.21.0.jar from Maven Central into your local repository, puts it on the classpath and compiles both classes: [INFO] --- compiler:3.13.0:compile (default-compile) @ my-app --- [INFO] Compiling 2 source files with javac [debug release 17] to target/classes ... [INFO] BUILD SUCCESS If the compiler reports package org.apache.commons.lang3 does not exist , the dependency is in the wrong <dependencies> element: move it out of <dependencyManagement> . Commons Lang needs no other libraries. When a library does, its own POM says so, and Maven downloads those libraries as well; How dependencies work explains these transitive dependencies.

title: 5. Run the program with its dependency
text: Run the program from the JAR as before: java -cp target/my-app-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar com.mycompany.app.App Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError:
terms: java target dependency mvn copy-dependencies DincludeScope runtime Hello Ada World
body: Run the program from the JAR as before: java -cp target/my-app-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar com.mycompany.app.App Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: org/apache/commons/lang3/StringUtils The JAR contains only your own classes. Maven puts the libraries on the classpath when it compiles and tests, but when you start the program yourself, you have to give them to java . Copy them into target/dependency , leaving out the libraries that are only for tests: mvn dependency:copy-dependencies -DincludeScope = runtime Then run the program with the JAR and the libraries on the classpath, and a name: java -cp "target/my-app-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar:target/dependency/*" com.mycompany.app.App ada Hello, Ada! Without a name, it prints Hello, World! . On Windows, separate the two classpath entries with ; instead of : . You now have a program that uses a library from Maven Central, and Maven downloads that library for anyone who builds the project.

title: Build an existing project
text: The vast majority of Maven-built projects can be built with the following command: mvn verify This command tells Maven to build all the subprojects, and to chec
body: The vast majority of Maven-built projects can be built with the following command: mvn verify This command tells Maven to build all the subprojects, and to check if all integration tests succeeded (when any was defined). That's it! If you look in the target subdirectory, you should find the build output and the final library or application that was being built. Note: Some projects have multiple subprojects, so the library or application you are looking for may be in a subproject's subdirectory. While this will build most projects and Maven encourages this standard convention, builds can be customisable. If this does not suffice, please consult the project's documentation.

title: More than just the Build
text: Maven can do more than just build software - it can assist with testing, run web applications and produce reports on projects, as well as any number of other ta
body: Maven can do more than just build software - it can assist with testing, run web applications and produce reports on projects, as well as any number of other tasks provided by plug-ins.

title: When Things go Wrong
text: The following are some common problems when building with Maven, and how to resolve them. Missing Dependencies A missing dependency presents with an error like
body: The following are some common problems when building with Maven, and how to resolve them. Missing Dependencies A missing dependency presents with an error like the following: [INFO] Failed to resolve artifact. Missing: ---------- 1) jnuit:junit:jar:3.8.1 Try downloading the file manually from the project website. Then, install it using the command: mvn install:install-file -DgroupId=jnuit -DartifactId=junit \ -Dversion=3.8.1 -Dpackaging=jar -Dfile=/path/to/file Path to dependency: 1) org.apache.maven:maven:pom:2.1-SNAPSHOT 2) jnuit:junit:jar:3.8.1 ---------- 1 required artifact is missing. for artifact: org.apache.maven:maven:pom:2.1-SNAPSHOT from the specified remote repositories: central (https://repo.maven.apache.org/maven2) To resolve this issue, it depends on what the dependency is and why it is missing. The most common cause is because it can not be redistributed from the repository and must be manually installed using the instructions given in the message. This is most common with some older JARs from Sun (usually javax.* group IDs), and is further documented in the Guide to Coping with Sun JARs . You can check the list of repositories at the end of the error to ensure that the expected ones are listed - it may be that the project requires an alternative repository that has not been declared properly or is not accessible with your Maven configuration. In other cases, it may be an incorrectly declared dependency (like the typo in the example above) which the project would need to fix, like a compilation error. Inconsistent output Most plugins are optimized to know if they have to execute their task. In some cases, the output can be polluted from a previous build and the end result is not what you expected. In such rare situations, you can call the clean phase which means: remove the output directory. You can also call it as mvn clean verify which means: first clean up the output directory, next build the project and verify the outcome.

title: Phases, goals and plugins
text: How Maven turns a command such as mvn package into a series of plugin goals, and why every Maven project builds with the same few commands.
keywords: build lifecycle default lifecycle clean lifecycle site lifecycle mojo plugin binding default bindings execution order before: after: why does package run tests Version not locked for default bindings plugins
terms: mvn package mvn verify mvn install mvn clean <packaging> <executions> <phase> <goal> <pluginManagement> integration-test pre-integration-test post-integration-test mvn package verify
body: Every Maven project builds with the same commands. mvn package makes a JAR of a library and a WAR of a web application; mvn verify builds and checks either one. The person who runs the build says how far the build should go. The project decides what happens on the way there. Three ideas make that split work: the lifecycle, its phases, and the plugin goals bound to those phases.

title: A lifecycle is a fixed list of phases
text: Maven has three lifecycles. The default lifecycle builds, tests and ships the project. The clean lifecycle removes what an earlier build produced. The site life
terms: validate compile test package verify install deploy generate-sources process-resources test-compile prepare-package mvn clean
body: Maven has three lifecycles. The default lifecycle builds, tests and ships the project. The clean lifecycle removes what an earlier build produced. The site lifecycle generates the project's website. Each lifecycle is a list of phases in a fixed order. The phases of the default lifecycle that you call from the command line are: Phase What happens validate Check that the project is complete and correct. compile Compile the source code. test Run the unit tests against the compiled code. package Package the compiled code, for example into a JAR file. verify Run integration tests and other checks on the package. install Copy the package into the local repository, for other projects on your machine. deploy Copy the package to a remote repository, for other people. Between these are phases such as generate-sources , process-resources , test-compile and prepare-package . The lifecycles reference lists every phase of the three lifecycles. When you name a phase, Maven runs all phases before it in the same lifecycle first. That is why mvn package runs the tests: test comes before package , and a JAR is only made from code that passed its tests. It is also why one command is enough. mvn install compiles, tests, packages and verifies before it installs, so there is no need to call each step. You can name phases of different lifecycles in one command. mvn clean package runs the clean lifecycle up to clean , and then the default lifecycle up to package .

title: Call verify, not integration-test
text: The phases whose names start with pre- , post- or process- prepare or finish the work of the phase next to them. They produce intermediate results, and you do n
terms: pre- post- process- pre-integration-test integration-test post-integration-test verify mvn before after compile prepare-package package process-classes sources resources ready
body: The phases whose names start with pre- , post- or process- prepare or finish the work of the phase next to them. They produce intermediate results, and you do not normally call them. Integration tests show why. A plugin that starts a server for the tests binds a goal to pre-integration-test , the tests run in integration-test , and the server is stopped in post-integration-test . Reports are checked in verify . In Maven 3, mvn integration-test stops after the integration-test phase: the server keeps running and no report is checked. mvn verify runs the whole sequence, which is why it is the command to call when you want to know whether the project builds and works. Maven 4: The default lifecycle is a tree of phases, each with a before: and an after: step, such as before:compile and after:compile . The Maven 3 names remain as aliases: prepare-package is before:package , process-classes is after:compile , pre-integration-test and post-integration-test are before:integration-test and after:integration-test . When you call a phase, Maven 4 runs its after: step as well. mvn integration-test therefore also runs post-integration-test , mvn compile also runs process-classes , and mvn prepare-package runs up to and including package . Maven 4 also adds phases such as sources , resources and ready (compiled and ready to use). The Maven 4 lifecycles reference lists them.

title: Plugin goals do the work
text: A phase is a name for a step. It does nothing by itself. The work is done by plugins: each plugin is a Java library with one or more goals, and each goal is one
terms: compile testCompile compiler default-compile my-app prefix goal mvn dependency tree clean copy-dependencies package DskipTests test Tests are skipped.
body: A phase is a name for a step. It does nothing by itself. The work is done by plugins: each plugin is a Java library with one or more goals, and each goal is one task. The Compiler plugin has a compile goal for your code and a testCompile goal for your tests. When a goal is bound to a phase, it runs every time the build passes that phase. A phase with no goal bound to it is skipped without notice. The build output names each goal it runs: [INFO] --- compiler:3.13.0:compile (default-compile) @ my-app --- This line reads as: the compile goal of the plugin with prefix compiler , version 3.13.0, in the execution default-compile , for the project my-app . You can also run a goal on its own, with prefix:goal on the command line. mvn dependency:tree runs only the tree goal of the Dependency plugin, and no phases. Goals and phases mix: mvn clean dependency:copy-dependencies package cleans, then copies the dependencies, then runs the default lifecycle up to package , in that order. Options that seem to change the lifecycle usually belong to a goal. -DskipTests does not leave out the test phase; it tells the Surefire plugin's test goal to run no tests, and the goal logs Tests are skipped.

title: Plugin versions belong in the POM
text: The goals in the default bindings come from plugins whose version you did not choose. When the POM does not set one, Maven uses a default that belongs to the Ma
body: The goals in the default bindings come from plugins whose version you did not choose. When the POM does not set one, Maven uses a default that belongs to the Maven release: Maven 3.9.16 builds a JAR with maven-jar-plugin 3.5.0, Maven 3.10.0 with 3.5.1. The same project can then build differently on two machines. That is why the project from the quickstart archetype lists every plugin of the default bindings, with a version, in <build><pluginManagement> . Setting the versions there fixes them for every build of the project, whichever Maven runs it. Maven 4: Maven 4 warns when a plugin of the default bindings has no version in the POM: Version not locked for default bindings plugins [maven-resources-plugin, maven-compiler-plugin, ...], you should define versions in pluginManagement section of your pom.xml or parent .

title: Plugins in the POM add goals
text: To add a step to the build, you add a plugin to the <build> section of the POM, with an execution that names the goal. This makes the build also package the sou
terms: <build> jar-no-fork package mvn my-app-1.0-SNAPSHOT-sources.jar jar source <phase> verify phase>
body: To add a step to the build, you add a plugin to the <build> section of the POM, with an execution that names the goal. This makes the build also package the source code: pom.xml <build> <plugins> <plugin> <artifactId> maven-source-plugin </artifactId> <version> 3.4.0 </version> <executions> <execution> <goals> <goal> jar-no-fork </goal> </goals> </execution> </executions> </plugin> </plugins> </build> A goal declares the phase it belongs to by default. jar-no-fork belongs to package , so mvn package now writes my-app-1.0-SNAPSHOT-sources.jar next to the JAR. When several goals are bound to the same phase, the goals of the packaging run first, then the goals from the POM in the order they appear there; here, jar:jar runs before source:jar-no-fork . To bind a goal to another phase, name the phase in the execution with <phase>verify</phase> . A plugin can have several executions, each with its own goals, phase and configuration; Configuring plugins describes them.

title: The packaging decides the default goals
text: Which goals a phase runs depends first of all on the project's packaging, the <packaging> element of the POM. A project without one has packaging jar , and gets
terms: <packaging> jar process-resources resources compile compiler process-test-resources testResources test-compile testCompile test surefire package install deploy war pom mvn
body: Which goals a phase runs depends first of all on the project's packaging, the <packaging> element of the POM. A project without one has packaging jar , and gets these goals: Phase Goal process-resources resources:resources compile compiler:compile process-test-resources resources:testResources test-compile compiler:testCompile test surefire:test package jar:jar install install:install deploy deploy:deploy Packaging war binds the same goals, with war:war instead of jar:jar . Packaging pom , used for parent projects that only hold configuration, binds nothing but install:install and deploy:deploy , because there is nothing to compile. The plugin bindings reference lists the bindings for every packaging. So mvn package means "compile, test and make a JAR" in one project and "compile, test and make a WAR" in another, and you do not need to know which before you run it.

title: Split your application into modules
text: Turn my-app into a parent POM with a library module and an application module, build them together, and build one with what it needs.
keywords: multi-module multi-project monorepo submodule subproject parent POM aggregator Reactor Build Order Reactor Summary build one module Could not resolve dependencies library module
terms: <modules> <module> <subprojects> <parent> pom packaging ${project.version} -pl -am reactor my-app greeting Greeter app
body: In this tutorial you split my-app into two modules: greeting , a library with the Greeter class and its test, and app , the application that uses it and is packed into one JAR. The top directory gets a parent POM that holds what the modules share and builds them together. Start in the my-app directory as you left it at the end of Test and build your project . At the end of this tutorial it looks like this: my-app |-- .mvn |-- pom.xml |-- app | |-- pom.xml | `-- src/main/java/com/mycompany/app/App.java `-- greeting |-- pom.xml `-- src |-- main/java/com/mycompany/app/Greeter.java `-- test/java/com/mycompany/app/GreeterTest.java

title: Where to go from here
text: Aggregation and inheritance explains the two roles the parent POM plays, and Split a project into modules is the same work as a checklist for your own projects.
body: Aggregation and inheritance explains the two roles the parent POM plays, and Split a project into modules is the same work as a checklist for your own projects. The rest of the Docs section is grouped by subject: Dependencies and repositories, Multi-module projects, Java versions and toolchains, Plugins, extensions and tools, and Build recipes, each starting from what you did in these five tutorials.

title: 1. Move the code into module directories
text: Remove the output of earlier builds first, while pom.xml still describes the old project: mvn clean Then make a directory for each module, move all code into ap
body: Remove the output of earlier builds first, while pom.xml still describes the old project: mvn clean Then make a directory for each module, move all code into app , and move Greeter and its test on to greeting : mkdir -p app greeting/src/main/java/com/mycompany/app mv src app/ mv app/src/test greeting/src/ mv app/src/main/java/com/mycompany/app/Greeter.java greeting/src/main/java/com/mycompany/app/ Each module has the standard directory layout of its own. The .mvn directory stays at the top: it marks the top directory of the whole project.

title: 2. Turn the top POM into a parent
text: In pom.xml in the my-app directory, add <packaging>pom</packaging> after the version and a <modules> list after <url> . Remove the Commons Lang dependency and t
terms: my-app <packaging> pom packaging> <modules> <url> <plugins> groupId version maven.compiler.release <pluginManagement>
body: In pom.xml in the my-app directory, add <packaging>pom</packaging> after the version and a <modules> list after <url> . Remove the Commons Lang dependency and the <plugins> element with the Shade plugin; they move to the modules. The file now reads: pom.xml <project ... > <modelVersion> 4.0.0 </modelVersion> <groupId> com.mycompany.app </groupId> <artifactId> my-app </artifactId> <version> 1.0-SNAPSHOT </version> <packaging> pom </packaging> <name> my-app </name> <!-- FIXME change it to the project's website --> <url> http://www.example.com </url> <modules> <module> greeting </module> <module> app </module> </modules> <properties> ... </properties> <dependencyManagement> ... </dependencyManagement> <dependencies> <dependency> <groupId> org.junit.jupiter </groupId> <artifactId> junit-jupiter-api </artifactId> <scope> test </scope> </dependency> ... </dependencies> <build> <pluginManagement> ... </pluginManagement> </build> </project> Packaging pom means that this project builds no JAR of its own. <modules> lists the directories of the modules, and makes Maven build them whenever you build this project. This POM is also the parent of both modules. They inherit its groupId and version , its properties such as maven.compiler.release , the plugin versions in <pluginManagement> and the JUnit dependencies, so either module can have tests.

title: 3. Write the POM of the library
text: Create a POM for greeting . It names my-app as its parent and adds the dependency its code needs: greeting/pom.xml <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?> <proje
body: Create a POM for greeting . It names my-app as its parent and adds the dependency its code needs: greeting/pom.xml <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?> <project xmlns= "http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0" xmlns:xsi= "http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xsi:schemaLocation= "http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 http://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd" > <modelVersion> 4.0.0 </modelVersion> <parent> <groupId> com.mycompany.app </groupId> <artifactId> my-app </artifactId> <version> 1.0-SNAPSHOT </version> </parent> <artifactId> greeting </artifactId> <dependencies> <dependency> <groupId> org.apache.commons </groupId> <artifactId> commons-lang3 </artifactId> <version> 3.21.0 </version> </dependency> </dependencies> </project> The module only declares its artifactId ; the rest of its coordinates come from the parent. Maven finds the parent's POM in the directory above, where it looks first.

title: 4. Write the POM of the application
text: Create a POM for app . It depends on greeting and gets the Shade plugin from Add and configure your first plugin : app/pom.xml <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF
terms: app greeting project.version <subprojects> <subproject> <modules> <parent <version> Unrecognised tag subprojects
body: Create a POM for app . It depends on greeting and gets the Shade plugin from Add and configure your first plugin : app/pom.xml <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?> <project xmlns= "http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0" xmlns:xsi= "http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xsi:schemaLocation= "http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 http://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd" > <modelVersion> 4.0.0 </modelVersion> <parent> <groupId> com.mycompany.app </groupId> <artifactId> my-app </artifactId> <version> 1.0-SNAPSHOT </version> </parent> <artifactId> app </artifactId> <dependencies> <dependency> <groupId> com.mycompany.app </groupId> <artifactId> greeting </artifactId> <version> ${project.version} </version> </dependency> </dependencies> <build> <plugins> <plugin> <artifactId> maven-shade-plugin </artifactId> <version> 3.6.2 </version> <executions> <execution> <phase> package </phase> <goals> <goal> shade </goal> </goals> <configuration> <transformers> <transformer implementation= "org.apache.maven.plugins.shade.resource.ManifestResourceTransformer" > <mainClass> com.mycompany.app.App </mainClass> </transformer> </transformers> <createDependencyReducedPom> false </createDependencyReducedPom> </configuration> </execution> </executions> </plugin> </plugins> </build> </project> A module uses another module through an ordinary dependency on its coordinates. ${project.version} is the version of this project, so app always uses the greeting of the same version. app gets Commons Lang through greeting , without declaring it. Maven 4: With model version 4.1.0, which only Maven 4 reads, the POMs can be shorter. The parent lists <subprojects> with one <subproject> per directory instead of <modules> , a module names its parent with an empty <parent/> , and app can leave out the <version> of greeting : app/pom.xml <project xmlns= "http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.1.0" xmlns:xsi= "http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xsi:schemaLocation= "http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.1.0 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.1.0.xsd" > <modelVersion> 4.1.0 </modelVersion> <parent/> <artifactId> app </artifactId> <dependencies> <dependency> <groupId> com.mycompany.app </groupId> <artifactId> greeting </artifactId> </dependency> </dependencies> ... </project> Maven 3 stops on such a POM with Unrecognised tag: 'subprojects' . Split a project into modules shows the parent POM in this form.

title: 5. Build all modules
text: In the my-app directory, run: mvn clean verify Maven reads the parent POM, finds the modules, and puts all three projects in an order in which every project com
terms: my-app mvn clean verify greeting app target java -jar app-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar ada Hello Ada
body: In the my-app directory, run: mvn clean verify Maven reads the parent POM, finds the modules, and puts all three projects in an order in which every project comes after the projects it needs. It prints that order first: [INFO] Reactor Build Order: [INFO] [INFO] my-app [pom] [INFO] greeting [jar] [INFO] app [jar] Then it builds them one after the other, in one run: it tests greeting and makes its JAR, and then compiles app against that JAR and packs both, with Commons Lang, into one. The summary at the end lists each project: [INFO] Reactor Summary for my-app 1.0-SNAPSHOT: [INFO] [INFO] my-app ............................................. SUCCESS [ 0.510 s] [INFO] greeting ........................................... SUCCESS [ 1.180 s] [INFO] app ................................................ SUCCESS [ 0.256 s] [INFO] ------------------------------------------------------------------------ [INFO] BUILD SUCCESS The part of Maven that builds several projects together is called the reactor. Each module has its own target directory. Run the application from the JAR of app : java -jar app/target/app-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar ada Hello, Ada!

title: 6. Build one module and what it needs
text: You can build part of the project from the top directory with -pl , short for --projects , followed by the module's directory. Start from nothing and try app al
terms: -pl --projects app mvn clean verify greeting NOT allowed from central -am --also-make my-app target project-local-repo
body: You can build part of the project from the top directory with -pl , short for --projects , followed by the module's directory. Start from nothing and try app alone: mvn clean mvn -pl app verify [ERROR] Failed to execute goal on project app: Could not resolve dependencies for project com.mycompany.app:app:jar:1.0-SNAPSHOT [ERROR] dependency: com.mycompany.app:greeting:jar:1.0-SNAPSHOT (compile) greeting is not part of this build, so Maven looks for it in the local repository, as for any other dependency, and you never installed it. The line after these two gives a reason that differs between Maven versions: Maven 3.10 and 4 say the path is NOT allowed from central , which only means that Maven Central has no such library. Add -am , short for --also-make , to build the module together with the modules it needs: mvn -pl app -am verify [INFO] Reactor Summary for my-app 1.0-SNAPSHOT: [INFO] [INFO] my-app ............................................. SUCCESS [ 0.001 s] [INFO] greeting ........................................... SUCCESS [ 1.695 s] [INFO] app ................................................ SUCCESS [ 0.273 s] [INFO] ------------------------------------------------------------------------ [INFO] BUILD SUCCESS Maven builds greeting because app depends on it, and the parent my-app because app inherits from it. Here that is the whole project; in a larger project, -am leaves out the modules that app does not need. Build part of a multi-module project shows the other ways to select modules. Maven 4: When Maven 4 packages a module, it keeps a copy of the JAR in .mvn/target/project-local-repo . After a full mvn verify , mvn -pl app verify finds greeting there and succeeds; mvn clean removes the copies, so the build above fails on Maven 4 as well. You now have a project of two modules that build together with one command, and you can build one of them with what it needs.

body: In Test and build your project you write a test for Greeter and see what the build does when it fails. Phases, goals and plugins explains how goals and phases fit together, and Configuring plugins covers configuration in full.

page: Add and configure your first plugin
title: 1. Try to run the JAR on its own
text: Run the JAR the way Java runs an application: java -jar target/my-app-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar no main manifest attribute, in target/my-app-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar java -jar r
body: Run the JAR the way Java runs an application: java -jar target/my-app-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar no main manifest attribute, in target/my-app-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar java -jar reads the name of the class to start from the JAR's manifest, the file META-INF/MANIFEST.MF inside the JAR, and this JAR names none. It also has no room for Commons Lang: java -jar ignores -cp , so the library has to be inside the JAR.

page: Add and configure your first plugin
title: 2. Find the plugin
text: Everything a Maven build does, a plugin does. Your build already uses several: the Compiler plugin compiles, the Surefire plugin runs the tests and the JAR plug
body: Everything a Maven build does, a plugin does. Your build already uses several: the Compiler plugin compiles, the Surefire plugin runs the tests and the JAR plugin makes the JAR. They come with the project's packaging, jar . For anything else, you add a plugin. The list of plugins names the plugins of the Maven project. The Shade plugin packs a project and its dependencies into one JAR, and can write the main class into the manifest. Its site lists the plugin's goals and has examples; this tutorial follows its "Executable JAR" example. The current version is 3.6.2, which works with Maven 3.9, 3.10 and 4.

page: Add and configure your first plugin
title: 3. Add the plugin to the build
text: Add a <plugins> element to <build> in pom.xml , after </pluginManagement> : pom.xml <project ... > ... <build> <pluginManagement> ... </pluginManagement> <plugi
terms: <plugins> <build> pluginManagement> <pluginManagement> <artifactId> <version> <groupId> org.apache.maven.plugins shade <execution> package mvn clean target default my-app-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar dependency Hello Ada original-my-app-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar
body: Add a <plugins> element to <build> in pom.xml , after </pluginManagement> : pom.xml <project ... > ... <build> <pluginManagement> ... </pluginManagement> <plugins> <plugin> <artifactId> maven-shade-plugin </artifactId> <version> 3.6.2 </version> <executions> <execution> <phase> package </phase> <goals> <goal> shade </goal> </goals> </execution> </executions> </plugin> </plugins> </build> </project> A plugin in <pluginManagement> only gets a version; a plugin in <plugins> becomes part of the build. <artifactId> and <version> say which plugin and which release of it. The <groupId> can be left out for the plugins of the Maven project, because Maven assumes org.apache.maven.plugins . A plugin does its work in goals, and the Shade plugin's goal is shade . The <execution> binds that goal to the package phase: every build that reaches package now runs shade , right after the JAR plugin has made the JAR. Build the project with: mvn clean package clean deletes the target directory before the build. Use it from now on: the Shade plugin replaces the JAR with its own, and when nothing changed since the last build, the JAR plugin keeps that JAR, Shade gets its own output as input, and it warns about hundreds of overlapping classes. The build now ends with the Shade plugin: [INFO] --- jar:3.4.2:jar (default-jar) @ my-app --- [INFO] Building jar: /home/you/projects/my-app/target/my-app-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar [INFO] [INFO] --- shade:3.6.2:shade (default) @ my-app --- [INFO] Dependency-reduced POM written at: /home/you/projects/my-app/dependency-reduced-pom.xml [WARNING] commons-lang3-3.21.0.jar, my-app-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar define 1 overlapping resource: [WARNING] - META-INF/MANIFEST.MF ... [INFO] Replacing original artifact with shaded artifact. [INFO] ------------------------------------------------------------------------ [INFO] BUILD SUCCESS (default) is the name of the execution, because you gave it none. The warning says that both JARs have a manifest, and that the new JAR keeps only one; that is expected here. target/my-app-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar now holds the classes of Commons Lang as well, so the program runs without target/dependency , which clean removed: java -cp target/my-app-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar com.mycompany.app.App ada Hello, Ada! The JAR without the library is kept as target/original-my-app-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar .

page: Add and configure your first plugin
title: 4. Configure the main class
text: A goal has parameters, and you set them in a <configuration> element. Inside an <execution> , the configuration applies to that execution only. Add the main cla
body: A goal has parameters, and you set them in a <configuration> element. Inside an <execution> , the configuration applies to that execution only. Add the main class to the execution: pom.xml <execution> <phase> package </phase> <goals> <goal> shade </goal> </goals> <configuration> <transformers> <transformer implementation= "org.apache.maven.plugins.shade.resource.ManifestResourceTransformer" > <mainClass> com.mycompany.app.App </mainClass> </transformer> </transformers> </configuration> </execution> The transformers parameter takes a list of transformers, which change files while the Shade plugin copies them into the JAR. ManifestResourceTransformer writes the main class into the manifest. Build and run the JAR: mvn clean package java -jar target/my-app-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar ada Hello, Ada!

page: Add and configure your first plugin
title: 5. Look up a parameter
text: List the my-app directory: ls dependency-reduced-pom.xml pom.xml src target The Shade plugin wrote dependency-reduced-pom.xml : a copy of your POM without the d
terms: my-app ls dependency-reduced-pom.xml pom.xml src target createDependencyReducedPom true false <transformers> rm mvn clean package Dependency-reduced POM written at java -jar my-app-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar ada Hello Ada
body: List the my-app directory: ls dependency-reduced-pom.xml pom.xml src target The Shade plugin wrote dependency-reduced-pom.xml : a copy of your POM without the dependencies that are now inside the JAR, for projects that use the JAR as a library. An application does not need it. To find out whether a plugin can leave something out, look at its goal. On the plugin's site, under "Plugin Documentation", the page of shade:shade lists every parameter of the goal, with its type, its default value and what it does. One of them is createDependencyReducedPom , default true . Set it to false in the configuration, next to <transformers> . The plugin now reads: pom.xml <plugin> <artifactId> maven-shade-plugin </artifactId> <version> 3.6.2 </version> <executions> <execution> <phase> package </phase> <goals> <goal> shade </goal> </goals> <configuration> <transformers> <transformer implementation= "org.apache.maven.plugins.shade.resource.ManifestResourceTransformer" > <mainClass> com.mycompany.app.App </mainClass> </transformer> </transformers> <createDependencyReducedPom> false </createDependencyReducedPom> </configuration> </execution> </executions> </plugin> Delete the file and build again: rm dependency-reduced-pom.xml mvn clean package The line Dependency-reduced POM written at is gone from the output, and so is the file. java -jar target/my-app-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar ada still prints Hello, Ada! . You now have a build that makes a JAR you can hand to anyone with Java, and you know where to look up what a plugin can do.

title: Create your first project
text: Check Java and Maven, generate a project from the quickstart archetype, build it into a JAR and run the program.
keywords: hello world new project quickstart first build five minutes mvn -v JAVA_HOME BUILD SUCCESS skeleton scaffold java -cp getting started prefixes file appears stale
terms: mvn --version archetype:generate maven-archetype-quickstart mvn package pom.xml target my-app
body: In this tutorial you create a small Java project with Maven, build it into a JAR file and run the program. It is the first of five tutorials that grow this one project, my-app , into an application with a library, a test and two modules. You need a terminal, an internet connection and a Java Development Kit (JDK) 17 or later.

title: 1. Check Java and Maven
text: Open a terminal and check which Java you have: java -version openjdk version "21.0.12.1" 2026-08-18 LTS ... The project you generate in the next step is compile

body: Open a terminal and check which Java you have: java -version openjdk version "21.0.12.1" 2026-08-18 LTS ... The project you generate in the next step is compiled for Java 17, so the version must be 17 or higher. Then check Maven: mvn --version Apache Maven 3.10.0 (c43a36b8d67be7e0805a411bc0898af1a51f5472) Maven home: /opt/apache-maven-3.10.0 Java version: 21.0.12.1, vendor: Eclipse Adoptium, runtime: /usr/lib/jvm/temurin-21 Default locale: en_US, platform encoding: UTF-8, time zone: Europe/Amsterdam OS name: "linux", version: "6.17.0", arch: "amd64", family: "unix" The first line shows the Maven version. Java version shows the JDK that Maven runs on, and that JDK also compiles your code. Maven uses the JDK in the JAVA_HOME environment variable, or the java on your PATH when JAVA_HOME is not set. If it shows a version older than 17, point JAVA_HOME at a newer JDK. If the shell cannot find mvn , install Maven first as described in Installation . Maven 4: Maven 4 itself needs Java 17 or later. With an older JDK, mvn stops with Error: Apache Maven 4.x requires Java 17 or newer to run. Maven 3.9 and 3.10 run on Java 8 and later, but this project still needs 17.

title: 2. Generate the project
text: Go to the directory where you keep your projects and run, on one line: mvn archetype:generate -DgroupId = com.mycompany.app -DartifactId = my-app -DarchetypeArt
terms: archetype generate maven-archetype-quickstart groupId artifactId DinteractiveMode false DarchetypeVersion Downloading from central m2 repository WARNING Don t override file archetype-catalog.xml
body: Go to the directory where you keep your projects and run, on one line: mvn archetype:generate -DgroupId = com.mycompany.app -DartifactId = my-app -DarchetypeArtifactId = maven-archetype-quickstart -DarchetypeVersion = 1.5 -DinteractiveMode = false An archetype is a project template. archetype:generate runs the generate goal of the Archetype plugin, which copies the template maven-archetype-quickstart , version 1.5, and fills in your groupId and artifactId . -DinteractiveMode=false makes it use the values on the command line instead of asking for them. Keep -DarchetypeVersion=1.5 : without it, you get version 1.0 of the template, which generates a project for JUnit 3. The first time, Maven prints many Downloading from central lines. It fetches the plugins it needs from Maven Central and keeps them in its local repository, the directory .m2/repository in your home directory, so later runs use those copies. The run ends with: [INFO] Project created from Archetype in dir: /home/you/projects/my-app [INFO] ------------------------------------------------------------------------ [INFO] BUILD SUCCESS [INFO] ------------------------------------------------------------------------ The three [WARNING] Don't override file lines before it are normal for this archetype. Maven 3.10 and 4 also print a warning that Maven Central's "prefixes file appears stale" for archetype-catalog.xml . It is about Maven Central's list of what it holds, not about your project, and you can ignore it.

title: 3. Look at the generated project
text: Go into the new directory: cd my-app It contains: my-app |-- .mvn | |-- jvm.config | `-- maven.config |-- pom.xml `-- src |-- main | `-- java | `-- com | `-- my
terms: cd my-app src main java test mvn groupId artifactId version SNAPSHOT maven.compiler.release project.build.sourceEncoding <dependencies> <build> <pluginManagement>
body: Go into the new directory: cd my-app It contains: my-app |-- .mvn | |-- jvm.config | `-- maven.config |-- pom.xml `-- src |-- main | `-- java | `-- com | `-- mycompany | `-- app | `-- App.java `-- test `-- java `-- com `-- mycompany `-- app `-- AppTest.java Your code goes in src/main/java and your tests in src/test/java . Maven knows where to look because every Maven project uses the same directory layout . The .mvn directory marks the top directory of the project; its two files are empty, and are where you can put options for Maven and for the JVM it runs in. pom.xml describes the project. It starts with the coordinates that identify the project, and two properties: pom.xml <project ... > <modelVersion> 4.0.0 </modelVersion> <groupId> com.mycompany.app </groupId> <artifactId> my-app </artifactId> <version> 1.0-SNAPSHOT </version> <name> my-app </name> <!-- FIXME change it to the project's website --> <url> http://www.example.com </url> <properties> <project.build.sourceEncoding> UTF-8 </project.build.sourceEncoding> <maven.compiler.release> 17 </maven.compiler.release> </properties> ... </project> groupId , artifactId and version together name what this project builds. A version that ends in -SNAPSHOT is still in development. maven.compiler.release sets the Java version to compile for, and project.build.sourceEncoding the encoding of your source files. The rest of the file has two parts. <dependencies> lists the libraries the project uses, here JUnit Jupiter for the tests. <build> contains a <pluginManagement> section that fixes the version of each plugin the build uses, so the project builds the same way whichever Maven version runs it. The program prints a greeting: src/main/java/com/mycompany/app/App.java public class App { public static void main ( String [] args ) { System . out . println ( "Hello World!" ); } } AppTest.java in src/test/java is a test that checks nothing yet. You replace it with a real one in Test and build your project .

title: 4. Build the project
text: In the my-app directory, run: mvn package Maven compiles the code, runs the test, and packages the classes into a JAR file. The output shows one line for each s
terms: my-app mvn package target classes test-classes surefire-reports my-app-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar
body: In the my-app directory, run: mvn package Maven compiles the code, runs the test, and packages the classes into a JAR file. The output shows one line for each step, after the downloads: [INFO] --- resources:3.3.1:resources (default-resources) @ my-app --- [INFO] --- compiler:3.13.0:compile (default-compile) @ my-app --- [INFO] Compiling 1 source file with javac [debug release 17] to target/classes [INFO] --- resources:3.3.1:testResources (default-testResources) @ my-app --- [INFO] --- compiler:3.13.0:testCompile (default-testCompile) @ my-app --- [INFO] --- surefire:3.3.0:test (default-test) @ my-app --- [INFO] Tests run: 1, Failures: 0, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0 [INFO] --- jar:3.4.2:jar (default-jar) @ my-app --- [INFO] Building jar: /home/you/projects/my-app/target/my-app-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar [INFO] ------------------------------------------------------------------------ [INFO] BUILD SUCCESS package is a phase of the build, not a single task: Maven runs every phase before it as well, from compiling to testing, and then makes the JAR. Phases, goals and plugins explains how that works. Everything Maven produces goes into the target directory: the compiled classes in target/classes , the compiled tests in target/test-classes , the test reports in target/surefire-reports and the JAR, target/my-app-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar .

title: 5. Run the program
text: Run the App class from the JAR: java -cp target/my-app-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar com.mycompany.app.App Hello World! You now have a Maven project that compiles, tests and
body: Run the App class from the JAR: java -cp target/my-app-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar com.mycompany.app.App Hello World! You now have a Maven project that compiles, tests and packages itself with one command.
