title: Select a JDK without toolchains.xml
text: Since version 3.2.0, the toolchains plugin can find the JDKs installed on your machine by itself. It looks in JAVA_HOME and in variables such as JAVA17_HOME , a
terms: JAVA_HOME JAVA17_HOME mvn toolchains display-discovered-jdk-toolchains select-jdk-toolchain toolchain toolchain.jdk.version
body: Since version 3.2.0, the toolchains plugin can find the JDKs installed on your machine by itself. It looks in JAVA_HOME and in variables such as JAVA17_HOME , and in the directories where SDKMAN!, IntelliJ IDEA, Gradle, asdf, jenv and the operating system's packages put JDKs. List what it finds: mvn toolchains:display-discovered-jdk-toolchains [INFO] Discovered 4 JDK toolchains: [INFO] - /home/me/.sdkman/candidates/java/21.0.12+1.1-tem [INFO] provides: [INFO] version: 21.0.12.1 [INFO] runtime.name: OpenJDK Runtime Environment [INFO] runtime.version: 21.0.12.1+1-LTS [INFO] vendor: Eclipse Adoptium [INFO] vendor.version: Temurin-21.0.12.1+1 [INFO] current: true [INFO] lts: true [INFO] env: JAVA_HOME [INFO] - /home/me/.sdkman/candidates/java/17.0.20-tem ... Then use the select-jdk-toolchain goal instead of toolchain , and give the version as a range in the toolchain.jdk.version property: pom.xml <properties> <toolchain.jdk.version> [17,18) </toolchain.jdk.version> </properties> <build> <plugins> <plugin> <groupId> org.apache.maven.plugins </groupId> <artifactId> maven-toolchains-plugin </artifactId> <version> 3.3.0 </version> <executions> <execution> <goals> <goal> select-jdk-toolchain </goal> </goals> </execution> </executions> </plugin> </plugins> </build> [INFO] --- toolchains:3.3.0:select-jdk-toolchain (default) @ my-app --- ... [INFO] Selected JDK toolchain: JDK[/home/me/.sdkman/candidates/java/17.0.20-tem] The version must be a range: a discovered JDK 17 has a version such as 17.0.20 , which a plain 17 does not match. Java 8 reports itself as 1.8.0_504 , so ask for it with [1.8,9) . When the JDK Maven runs on falls in the range, the goal keeps that JDK and selects no toolchain; [17,) on Maven running on Java 21 builds with Java 21. The goal also uses the entries of toolchains.xml , and it remembers what it found in ~/.m2/discovered-jdk-toolchains-cache.xml . To try a JDK without changing the POM, run the goal from the command line before the phase: mvn toolchains:select-jdk-toolchain -Dtoolchain.jdk.version="[17,18)" verify The JDK discovery page of the plugin lists the other requirements it accepts, such as a vendor or an environment variable, and how it orders JDKs that all match.

page: Build with a different JDK than Maven runs on
title: Select the JDK in the POM
text: Add the maven-toolchains-plugin to the build with an execution of its toolchain goal, and state the JDK the project needs: pom.xml <build> <plugins> <plugin> <g
body: Add the maven-toolchains-plugin to the build with an execution of its toolchain goal, and state the JDK the project needs: pom.xml <build> <plugins> <plugin> <groupId> org.apache.maven.plugins </groupId> <artifactId> maven-toolchains-plugin </artifactId> <version> 3.3.0 </version> <executions> <execution> <goals> <goal> toolchain </goal> </goals> </execution> </executions> <configuration> <toolchains> <jdk> <version> 17 </version> </jdk> </toolchains> </configuration> </plugin> </plugins> </build> The goal runs in the validate phase, before anything is compiled. Add <vendor> next to <version> to require a vendor as well, or use a range such as [17,) to accept any JDK from 17 up; the first entry in toolchains.xml that matches is used. In a multi-module project, put the plugin in the parent POM so that every module is built with the same JDK. Set the release you compile for as usual, for example with the maven.compiler.release property. The toolchain decides which JDK compiles; release decides which Java version the classes are for.

page: Build with a different JDK than Maven runs on
title: Use another JDK for one plugin
text: To run only the tests on another JDK, give Surefire a requirement of its own with jdkToolchain . It is matched against toolchains.xml and overrides the JDK sele
body: To run only the tests on another JDK, give Surefire a requirement of its own with jdkToolchain . It is matched against toolchains.xml and overrides the JDK selected for the module. Compile for an older Java version shows it for tests on Java 8.

page: Compile for an older Java version
title: Compile for an older Java version
text: Build classes that run on an older Java than the JDK you build with, check them against that Java's API, and run the tests on it.
keywords: Java 8 Java 11 older JDK target version cross-compile javac --release -source -target class file version major version javap UnsupportedClassVersionError NoSuchMethodError bootstrap class path not set
terms: maven.compiler.release <release> maven.compiler.source maven.compiler.target maven-compiler-plugin jdkToolchain maven-surefire-plugin
body: Use this when your code has to run on an older Java than the JDK you build with, for example a library that still supports Java 8 while you build on JDK 21. The compiler of a newer JDK can do this by itself; you only need a second JDK to run the tests on the older Java.

page: Compile for an older Java version
title: Run the tests on the older Java
text: release proves that the code compiles against the older API, not that it behaves the same on the older runtime. To run the tests on Java 8, describe a Java 8 JD
body: release proves that the code compiles against the older API, not that it behaves the same on the older runtime. To run the tests on Java 8, describe a Java 8 JDK in ~/.m2/toolchains.xml : ~/.m2/toolchains.xml <toolchains> <toolchain> <type> jdk </type> <provides> <version> 1.8 </version> </provides> <configuration> <jdkHome> /opt/jdk/temurin-8 </jdkHome> </configuration> </toolchain> </toolchains> and give Surefire that JDK with jdkToolchain : pom.xml <plugin> <groupId> org.apache.maven.plugins </groupId> <artifactId> maven-surefire-plugin </artifactId> <version> 3.6.0 </version> <configuration> <jdkToolchain> <version> 1.8 </version> </jdkToolchain> </configuration> </plugin> The code is compiled by the JDK Maven runs on and tested on Java 8: [INFO] Compiling 1 source file with javac [debug release 8] to target/classes ... [INFO] Toolchain in maven-surefire-plugin: JDK[/opt/jdk/temurin-8] jdkToolchain needs Surefire 3.0.0-M5 or later and is matched against toolchains.xml only. The version in it must match the <version> of the entry exactly, here 1.8 ; use a range such as [1.8,9) to accept any Java 8 entry. Failsafe has the same parameter for integration tests. The test libraries must run on Java 8 as well: JUnit 6 needs Java 17, so tests on Java 8 use JUnit 5. To run the whole build on the older JDK instead, compiler included, select it for the module with the toolchains plugin as in Build with a different JDK than Maven runs on . With a Java 8 toolchain, the compiler plugin passes -source and -target instead of --release , because the javac of JDK 8 has no --release option; it compiles against the Java 8 class library either way.

page: Compile for an older Java version
title: Set the release
text: Set the maven.compiler.release property to the oldest Java version the code must run on: pom.xml <properties> <maven.compiler.release> 8 </maven.compiler.releas
terms: maven.compiler.release javac --release release version not supported javap target classes -v com example Greeter.class grep major
body: Set the maven.compiler.release property to the oldest Java version the code must run on: pom.xml <properties> <maven.compiler.release> 8 </maven.compiler.release> </properties> Or set it in the configuration of the compiler plugin, which has the same effect: pom.xml <plugin> <groupId> org.apache.maven.plugins </groupId> <artifactId> maven-compiler-plugin </artifactId> <version> 3.16.0 </version> <configuration> <release> 8 </release> </configuration> </plugin> The compiler plugin passes it to javac as --release 8 , and the build log shows it: [INFO] Compiling 1 source file with javac [debug release 8] to target/classes Use the plain version number, 8 ; with 1.8 the compiler stops with release version 1.8 not supported . The javac of JDK 21 adds warnings that source value 8 is obsolete and will be removed in a future release ; they do not stop the build. A JDK supports only a limited number of older releases: the javac of JDK 21 accepts 8 but stops with release version 7 not supported for 7 . For a release your JDK no longer supports, build with an older JDK as in Build with a different JDK than Maven runs on . To see which Java version a class was compiled for, read its class file version with javap from the target/classes directory: javap -v com/example/Greeter.class | grep major major version: 52 Java 8 11 17 21 25 Major version 52 55 61 65 69

page: Compile for an older Java version
title: UnsupportedClassVersionError
text: A class compiled for a newer Java than the one that runs it does not load: Exception in thread "main" java.lang.UnsupportedClassVersionError: com/example/Greete
body: A class compiled for a newer Java than the one that runs it does not load: Exception in thread "main" java.lang.UnsupportedClassVersionError: com/example/Greeter has been compiled by a more recent version of the Java Runtime (class file version 61.0), this version of the Java Runtime only recognizes class file versions up to 52.0 The class was compiled for Java 17 (61) and run on Java 8 (52). Lower release to the version that runs the code, or run it on a newer Java. When the class in the message belongs to a dependency, that dependency needs a newer Java than your release, and you need an older version of it.

page: Compile for an older Java version
title: Why source and target are not enough
text: The older maven.compiler.source and maven.compiler.target properties set the language level and the class file version, but the code is still compiled against t
terms: maven.compiler.source maven.compiler.target source target bootstrap class path not set in conjunction with -source release
body: The older maven.compiler.source and maven.compiler.target properties set the language level and the class file version, but the code is still compiled against the class library of the JDK that runs the compiler. Code that calls a method the older Java does not have compiles without an error: src/main/java/com/example/Greeter.java public String greet ( String name ) { if ( name . isBlank ()) { return "Hello" ; } return "Hello, " + name ; } With source and target 8 on JDK 21, the build succeeds with a warning that bootstrap class path not set in conjunction with -source 8 . The class says it is for Java 8, and fails only when Java 8 runs it: Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NoSuchMethodError: java.lang.String.isBlank()Z at com.example.Greeter.greet(Greeter.java:5) With release 8, the compiler checks the code against the Java 8 API and the build fails where the problem is: [ERROR] /home/me/my-app/src/main/java/com/example/Greeter.java:[5,17] cannot find symbol [ERROR] symbol: method isBlank() [ERROR] location: variable name of type java.lang.String Replace source and target with release . When none of the three is set, the compiler plugin compiles with source and target 1.8.

title: toolchains.xml
text: Where Maven reads toolchains.xml, the elements of a JDK toolchain, how a requirement matches an entry, and which plugins use the selected toolchain.
keywords: toolchains file location global toolchains user toolchains version range vendor JDK discovery discovered-jdk-toolchains-cache.xml toolchain-aware plugins Misconfigured toolchains No toolchain matched
terms: toolchains.xml <toolchains> <toolchain> <type> <provides> <configuration> <jdkHome> -t --toolchains -gt --global-toolchains -it --install-toolchains maven.user.toolchains maven.installation.toolchains jdkToolchain select-jdk-toolchain toolchain.jdk.version
body: toolchains.xml describes the tools installed on a machine, most often JDKs, so that a build can ask for one without naming its path. Toolchains and the JDK Maven runs on explains the idea; Build with a different JDK than Maven runs on puts it to use.

title: Discovered JDK toolchains
text: The select-jdk-toolchain goal of the maven-toolchains-plugin, since version 3.2.0, matches its requirement against the entries of toolchains.xml and against the
terms: select-jdk-toolchain JAVA_HOME JAVA <n> HOME JAVA17_HOME bin javac version runtime.name OpenJDK Runtime Environment runtime.version vendor Eclipse Adoptium vendor.version Temurin-17.0.20 current true lts env toolchain.jdk.version toolchain.jdk.vendor runtimeName toolchain.jdk.runtime.name runtimeVersion toolchain.jdk.runtime.version toolchain.jdk.env
body: The select-jdk-toolchain goal of the maven-toolchains-plugin, since version 3.2.0, matches its requirement against the entries of toolchains.xml and against the JDKs it discovers. It finds JDKs through: the environment variables JAVA_HOME and JAVA<n>_HOME , such as JAVA17_HOME ; the JDK Maven runs on; the directories of installers in your home directory: .sdkman/candidates/java , .jdks , .m2/jdks , .gradle/jdks , .jenv/versions , .jbang/cache/jdks , .asdf/installs/java , .jabba/jdk , .local/share/mise/installs/java ; on macOS, /Library/Java/JavaVirtualMachines and ~/Library/Java/JavaVirtualMachines ; on Windows, the directories of Amazon Corretto, BellSoft, Eclipse Adoptium, Java and Zulu under C:\Program Files , and the JDKs installed with Scoop; on other systems, /usr/jdk , /usr/java , /usr/local/java , /opt/java , /usr/lib/jvm and /usr/lib64/jvm ; the tool cache of GitHub Actions runners. A directory without bin/javac is skipped. The goal keeps what it found in ~/.m2/discovered-jdk-toolchains-cache.xml . A discovered JDK provides these labels, read from the JDK itself: Label Example version 17.0.20 ; Java 8 reports 1.8.0_504 runtime.name OpenJDK Runtime Environment runtime.version 17.0.20+8 vendor Eclipse Adoptium vendor.version Temurin-17.0.20+8 current true for the JDK Maven runs on lts true for a long-term support release env The environment variables that point to it, such as JAVA17_HOME The goal takes its requirement from these parameters: Parameter Property Meaning version toolchain.jdk.version A version range, such as [17,18) . A single version such as 17 does not match 17.0.20 . vendor toolchain.jdk.vendor The vendor. runtimeName toolchain.jdk.runtime.name The runtime name. runtimeVersion toolchain.jdk.runtime.version The runtime version. env toolchain.jdk.env The name of an environment variable that must point to the JDK, such as JAVA17_HOME . useJdk toolchain.jdk.mode IfMatch (default): select no toolchain when the JDK Maven runs on matches. IfSame : select no toolchain when the best match is the JDK Maven runs on. Never : always select a toolchain. comparator toolchain.jdk.comparator The order of preference among matching JDKs. Default lts,current,env,version,vendor . discoverToolchains toolchain.jdk.discover false to use only the entries of toolchains.xml . Default true . The plugin's JDK discovery page and the description of the goal have the details. The goals display-discovered-jdk-toolchains and generate-jdk-toolchains-xml print the discovered JDKs, the second one in the format of toolchains.xml .

title: Elements
text: ~/.m2/toolchains.xml <toolchains> <toolchain> <type> jdk </type> <provides> <version> 17 </version> <vendor> temurin </vendor> </provides> <configuration> <jdkH
terms: <toolchains> <toolchain> <type> jdk protobuf <provides> <version> <vendor> <id> <configuration> <jdkHome> bin javac http maven.apache.org TOOLCHAINS
body: ~/.m2/toolchains.xml <toolchains> <toolchain> <type> jdk </type> <provides> <version> 17 </version> <vendor> temurin </vendor> </provides> <configuration> <jdkHome> /opt/jdk/temurin-17 </jdkHome> </configuration> </toolchain> </toolchains> Element Contains <toolchains> The root element. Zero or more <toolchain> elements. <toolchain> One installed tool. <type> The kind of tool. jdk for a JDK; plugins that bring their own toolchain type define other values, such as protobuf . <provides> Labels that requirements are matched against, one element per label: <version> , <vendor> , or any name you choose, such as <id> . The values are yours; Maven does not read them from the tool. <configuration> Where the tool is. Its content depends on the type. <jdkHome> For type jdk : the JDK's home directory, the directory that contains bin/javac . When it does not exist, the toolchains plugin stops with Misconfigured toolchains. Non-existing JDK home configuration at and the path. The root element may carry the namespace http://maven.apache.org/TOOLCHAINS/1.1.0 , which Maven 3 uses, or http://maven.apache.org/TOOLCHAINS/1.2.0 , which Maven 4 uses, or none. Maven 3.9, 3.10 and 4.0 read all three forms.

title: How requirements match
text: A requirement is the set of labels a project asks for, in the configuration of the toolchains plugin or in a plugin's jdkToolchain parameter: pom.xml <toolchain
body: A requirement is the set of labels a project asks for, in the configuration of the toolchains plugin or in a plugin's jdkToolchain parameter: pom.xml <toolchains> <jdk> <version> [11,18) </version> <vendor> temurin </vendor> </jdk> </toolchains> The element name, here jdk , is the toolchain type. Every label in the requirement must match the label of the same name in <provides> . Labels the requirement does not mention are not checked. version is compared as a version. A single version matches only the same version: 17 matches 17 , but not 17.0.20 , and 8 does not match 1.8 . A range, such as [17,18) , [11,) or (,11] , matches every version inside it: [17,18) matches 17 and 17.0.20 , and [1.8,9) matches 1.8 . Every other label is compared as text, ignoring case: Temurin matches temurin . When several toolchains match, the first one in the list is used: the user file before the global file, and within a file from top to bottom. When no toolchain matches, the toolchains plugin stops the build: [ERROR] No toolchain matched from 3 found for type jdk [ERROR] Cannot find matching toolchain definitions for the following toolchain types: jdk [ version='25' ]

title: Plugins that use toolchains
text: These plugins use the JDK toolchain selected for the module. The plugins with a version in the last column also accept a requirement of their own in a jdkToolch
terms: jdkToolchain Build-Jdk-Spec exec build protobuf protoc
body: These plugins use the JDK toolchain selected for the module. The plugins with a version in the last column also accept a requirement of their own in a jdkToolchain parameter, which overrides the module's selection for that plugin and is matched against toolchains.xml only. Plugin Uses the selected JDK since jdkToolchain since maven-compiler-plugin 2.1 3.6.0 maven-surefire-plugin 2.4.3 3.0.0-M5 maven-failsafe-plugin 2.5 3.0.0-M5 maven-javadoc-plugin 2.5 3.0.0 maven-jarsigner-plugin 1.3 maven-pmd-plugin 3.14.0 3.14.0 maven-jar-plugin , for the Build-Jdk-Spec manifest entry 3.4.0 maven-jlink-plugin 3.0.0-alpha-1 3.0.0-alpha-1 maven-jmod-plugin 3.0.0-alpha-1 3.0.0-alpha-1 maven-jdeps-plugin 3.0.0 maven-jdeprscan-plugin 3.0.0-alpha-1 exec-maven-plugin (MojoHaus), exec goal 1.1.1 animal-sniffer-maven-plugin (MojoHaus), build goal 1.3 cassandra-maven-plugin (MojoHaus) 0.7.0-1 keytool-maven-plugin (MojoHaus) 1.4 to 1.7; not in 2.x The protobuf-maven-plugin of org.xolstice uses a toolchain of type protobuf for the protoc compiler, since version 0.5.0. A plugin can define its own toolchain type; see Custom Toolchains .

title: Where Maven reads it
text: Maven reads two files and puts their toolchains in one list, those of the user file first. File Default location Command-line option Property User ~/.m2/toolcha
terms: -t --toolchains maven.user.toolchains -gt --global-toolchains The specified user toolchains file does not exist global -it --install-toolchains maven.installation.toolchains installation
body: Maven reads two files and puts their toolchains in one list, those of the user file first. File Default location Command-line option Property User ~/.m2/toolchains.xml -t , --toolchains maven.user.toolchains (Maven 4) Global conf/toolchains.xml in the Maven installation -gt , --global-toolchains A file in a default location that does not exist is skipped. A file named with -t or -gt must exist, or Maven stops with The specified user toolchains file does not exist or The specified global toolchains file does not exist . The global file that comes with Maven contains only comments, so out of the box all toolchains come from the user file. Maven 4: The global file is called the installation file. Its option is -it or --install-toolchains , and its property maven.installation.toolchains . -gt still works, with a warning that it is deprecated. A missing file named with either option stops Maven with The specified installation toolchains file does not exist .

page: Toolchains and the JDK Maven runs on
title: Toolchains and the JDK Maven runs on
text: Why Maven keeps the JDK it runs on apart from the JDK that compiles and tests your code, how plugins find that JDK, and how it differs from release.
keywords: JDK javac java version multiple JDKs different JDK build JDK runtime JDK Java 8 Java 11 Java 17 project SDK cross-compile --release
terms: toolchains.xml maven-toolchains-plugin JAVA_HOME jdkToolchain select-jdk-toolchain maven.compiler.release mvn java javadoc
body: Maven is a Java program. The mvn command starts it on the JDK that JAVA_HOME points to, or on the java command on your path when JAVA_HOME is not set. Unless you say otherwise, every plugin that needs a JDK tool takes it from that same JDK: the compiler plugin compiles with its compiler, Surefire starts the tests with its java , and the Javadoc plugin runs its javadoc . The JDK that runs Maven and the JDK that builds your code are then the same JDK.

page: Toolchains and the JDK Maven runs on
title: How a plugin finds its toolchain
text: Selecting a toolchain and using it are the work of different plugins. The maven-toolchains-plugin runs at the start of the build, in the validate phase. Its too
terms: validate toolchain select-jdk-toolchain jdk javac Found matching for type Toolchain in maven-compiler-plugin jdkToolchain
body: Selecting a toolchain and using it are the work of different plugins. The maven-toolchains-plugin runs at the start of the build, in the validate phase. Its toolchain goal compares the requirement in the POM with the toolchains in toolchains.xml . Its select-jdk-toolchain goal, available since version 3.2.0 of the plugin, also considers the JDKs it finds installed on the machine. Either goal stores the toolchain it selects in the build context of the module that is being built. Each toolchain-aware plugin that runs later asks that build context for a toolchain of type jdk . When there is one, the plugin takes its tools from that JDK: the compiler plugin starts the toolchain's javac in a separate process, and Surefire and Failsafe start the test JVM from it. When there is none, the plugin uses the JDK Maven runs on. The build log shows both halves, first Found matching toolchain for type jdk from the toolchains plugin, then a line such as Toolchain in maven-compiler-plugin from each plugin that uses it. Because the selection belongs to a module, a module in a multi-module build that does not run the toolchains plugin is built with Maven's own JDK. Configure the plugin in a parent POM to cover every module. A plugin that is not toolchain-aware ignores the selection altogether; the toolchains.xml reference lists the plugins that are. Several plugins, among them the compiler plugin, Surefire, Failsafe and the Javadoc plugin, also accept a requirement of their own in a jdkToolchain parameter. It overrides the module's selection for that one plugin, which is how a build compiles with one JDK and runs its tests on another. A plugin's own requirement is looked up in toolchains.xml only, not among the JDKs that select-jdk-toolchain discovers.

page: Toolchains and the JDK Maven runs on
title: Toolchains and the release option
text: The compiler's release option, set with the maven.compiler.release property, answers a different question: which Java version the compiled classes are for. The
body: The compiler's release option, set with the maven.compiler.release property, answers a different question: which Java version the compiled classes are for. The javac of JDK 21 with release 8 writes class files that Java 8 can load, and it rejects code that uses an API Java 8 does not have. If all you need is a library or application that runs on an older Java, release is enough, and Maven and the compiler can stay on the newer JDK. Compile for an older Java version shows how. You need a toolchain when something has to run on the older Java rather than be compiled for it: tests that should catch differences in the older runtime, or tools whose output depends on the JDK. You also need one when the newer compiler no longer supports the release you target: the javac of JDK 21 accepts release 8 but not 7. Most builds that select a toolchain still set release , so that the class files do not depend on which JDK happened to match.

page: Toolchains and the JDK Maven runs on
title: Two JDKs in one build
text: They do not have to be the same, and often should not be. Your project may have to be tested on Java 11 while you run Maven on Java 21. A team may want every bu
body: They do not have to be the same, and often should not be. Your project may have to be tested on Java 11 while you run Maven on Java 21. A team may want every build to use the JDK that production runs on, whatever each developer has as a default. A library may be compiled with the newest JDK and still have its tests run on the oldest Java it supports. Changing JAVA_HOME before each build works for one project at a time, but it also changes the JDK Maven itself runs on, it has to be repeated in every shell and on every build server, and nothing in the project records which JDK it needs. Maven 4: Maven 4 does not start on a Java version older than 17. To compile and test a project with Java 8 or 11 under Maven 4, you need a toolchain. Maven 3.9 and 3.10 run on Java 8 and later.

page: Toolchains and the JDK Maven runs on
title: What a toolchain is
text: A toolchain is a description of a tool installed on the machine: what type of tool it is, what it provides, and where it is. For a JDK that is the type jdk , a
body: A toolchain is a description of a tool installed on the machine: what type of tool it is, what it provides, and where it is. For a JDK that is the type jdk , a version and other labels such as a vendor, and the JDK's home directory. These descriptions live outside the project, in ~/.m2/toolchains.xml on each machine, because the paths differ from one machine to the next. The project only states what it needs: a JDK of version 17. It is the same split as in an IDE, where you register the JDKs installed on your computer once and each project picks one of them. At the start of the build Maven matches the project's requirement against the descriptions on the machine, and the build fails when none fits, instead of quietly using another JDK.

page: Toolchains and the JDK Maven runs on
title: Why not configure each plugin
text: Most plugins that use a JDK can also be pointed at one directly: the compiler plugin with fork and executable , Surefire with jvm , the Javadoc plugin with java
body: Most plugins that use a JDK can also be pointed at one directly: the compiler plugin with fork and executable , Surefire with jvm , the Javadoc plugin with javadocExecutable . That puts the path of a JDK in the POM, which is wrong on every machine but one unless you route it through a property, and it has to be repeated for every plugin. Miss one and your code is compiled with Java 17 but tested on Java 21, or the Javadoc is made by a third JDK. A toolchain is selected once, and every toolchain-aware plugin in the module uses it.

page: Toolchains and the JDK Maven runs on
title: Written down or discovered
text: There are two ways for Maven to know about the JDKs on a machine. In toolchains.xml you describe each JDK yourself. The labels in it are yours: Maven does not c
body: There are two ways for Maven to know about the JDKs on a machine. In toolchains.xml you describe each JDK yourself. The labels in it are yours: Maven does not check that the JDK in the directory you name is the version you wrote, only that the directory exists. A requirement of 17 matches an entry with the version 17 , so the labels in the file and the requirements in your POMs have to agree. In return you decide exactly which JDK a requirement selects, on every machine. The select-jdk-toolchain goal looks for JDKs where installers put them and in JAVA_HOME and JAVA17_HOME -style environment variables, and reads the real version and vendor of each one, such as 17.0.20 from Eclipse Adoptium. Nobody has to write a file per machine, but a version requirement has to be a range such as [17,18) , and when the JDK Maven runs on already satisfies it, that JDK is used and no toolchain is selected. Build with a different JDK than Maven runs on shows both.

title: Start with Maven 4 (migration)
text: Maven 4 introduces several updates and improvements (see "What's new in Maven 4?" ). Some of them are backwards compatible with Maven 3, but some require change
body: Maven 4 introduces several updates and improvements (see "What's new in Maven 4?" ). Some of them are backwards compatible with Maven 3, but some require changes of your build environment or Maven project. This page offers help for users who want to build their projects with Maven 4 (and check with RCs that everything is fine). In short, the general suggestion for the migration is to do it in three steps: prepare : Meet the prerequisites with latest Maven 3 test : Build in parallel with Maven 4 ( latest RC of Maven 4 ) and do minimal Maven 3-compatible fixes (report us if anything is unexpected) migrate : Drop Maven 3 and introduce optional Maven 4 features (see also Maven Upgrade Tool ) If you run into any issues, please don't hesitate to contact the users mailing list . The Maven team is interested in all your migration experiences - either good or bad! Many OSS projects have already published releases to Maven Central with Maven 4 RC : it's time to check that latest Maven 4 RC works for you before we release the long awaited Maven 4.0.0. Notes : This page will constantly be updated to contain changes, but also to integrate feedback of the community and their experience when upgrading to Maven 4 (RC). This means it will still receive updates after Maven 4 (RC or final) has been released. Since Maven 4.0.0-rc-4, Maven ships with a built-in migration tool for "step 3 -- migrate" (see Maven Upgrade Tool ), doing most of the steps needed to benefit from optional Maven 4 specific features. This guide does not contain information about how to update plugins to use the new Maven 4 plugin API. We plan to create a separate guide for this when we'll work on Maven 4.1: for now, we focus on using Maven 4.0.x (RC) with classical Maven 3 plugins. Table of content

title: Step 1 -- prepare: Maven 3 Prerequisites
text: This guide assumes that your environment and project meets the following prerequisites. If they don't, please make sure they do before continuing with this guid
body: This guide assumes that your environment and project meets the following prerequisites. If they don't, please make sure they do before continuing with this guide. Use latest version of Maven 3.9 This guide assumes that the project to be migrated was successfully built using the latest version of Maven 3 . Upgrade plugins to their latest Maven 3 version Similar to the previous prerequisite, the guides assumes that you are using the latest Maven 3 plugin version of all your plugins. Do not upgrade yet to a plugin version which requires Maven 4! Be aware of this, if you use tools that can automate updates. You can use the versions-maven-plugin's display-plugin-updates goal to see which are the latest available versions of the plugins you use. The following example shows the output of the Versions Maven Plugin in a project using the outdated version 3.12.0 of the Maven Compiler Plugin. As you can see, it shows that 3.14.0 is the best Maven 3 compatible update, while versions 4.0.0-beta-1 and 4.0.0-beta-2 require Maven 4 versions, not yet for the current step. title: Step 2 -- test: Minimal Updates for Maven 4
text: You need to do the following steps to be able to use Maven 4. Upgrade build environment to support Java 17 Maven 4 requires Java 17 to be run. This means the bu
body: You need to do the following steps to be able to use Maven 4. Upgrade build environment to support Java 17 Maven 4 requires Java 17 to be run. This means the build environment (locally but also your CI environment) needs to provide a JDK that supports Java 17. Either install one to your machine or use a container providing one. Note : Maven 3 can also be executed with Java 17. So you should prepare your build environment as soon as possible to have a solid, project independent base for further migration. Install and use Maven 4 After you have upgraded your build environment to support Java 17, you also need to provide Maven 4. See the information where to download and how to install Maven 4 for further information. Places where you might have to configure Maven 4 usage aside installation: Maven Wrapper 's maven-wrapper.properties file. Required Maven version rule of the Maven enforcer plugin. Your own CI/CD configuration scripts or pipelines. Update few necessary plugins to Maven 4 version If there is a dedicated Maven 4 version for used plugins, you should evaluate updating to such a version. You can use the Versions Maven Plugin's display-plugin-updates goal to check for updates. Note : Maven 4 aims to support all Maven 3.9 compatible plugins that do not use old Maven 2 APIs. This is why we promote upgrading to latest release, and to Maven 4 specific release only when a plugin requires definitively a Maven 4-specific update (a bugfix or a feature).

title: Step 3 -- migrate: Drop Maven 3, use Optional Maven 4 features
text: In this step, we'll update your project's pom.xml to benefit from new Maven 4 features that are not available in Maven 3: by applying required changes, you won'
terms: pom.xml installAtEnd deployAtEnd true false root project.rootDirectory mvn <subprojects> <modules> project.version revision install deploy bom <packaging> all each before after <sourceDirectory> <testSourceDirectory> <sources>
body: In this step, we'll update your project's pom.xml to benefit from new Maven 4 features that are not available in Maven 3: by applying required changes, you won't be able to build your project with Maven 3 any more. Notice that Maven 4 Consumer POM will automatically be triggered, which makes sure the output of your project can still be used by any tool, be it Maven 3 or other build tools: only building your project from pom.xml in your source control (aka. Build POM ) requires Maven 4. Changed default values Install/deploy at end of build (breaking change) Both, the Maven Install Plugin and the Maven Deploy Plugin, have changed default values for their behavior, about when to install respectively deploy. The default values for installAtEnd and deployAtEnd are set to true in Maven 4. They now reflect the desired behavior for the majority of the Maven builds. If you manually set these values to true before, you can remove the explicit declaration and inherit the same behavior from the new default values now. If your build relies on the old default value ( false ), you have to add it to your plugin configuration now. But in most cases, a build that requires the values to be false means that these settings hide a configuration error. We suggest to analyse the build configuration after migration. Use POM model version 4.1.0 Using POM model version 4.1.0 is not required with Maven 4.0.0. It is only required, for using new POM features like root -attribute, BOM packaging types, optional profiles and others. Model version 4.1.0 (or higher) will be required in future versions of Maven. It's suggested to migrate your project to Maven 4 without any POM changes that require model version 4.1.0 first. After you have successfully done this, include wanted features step by step. Define project's root directory It is highly recommended to define the project's root directory. While the definition is not enforced with Maven 4.0.0, it might be in the future. Some new Maven 4 features, for example the ${project.rootDirectory} property, do require it. When the root directory is not defined, the following warning is displayed: [WARNING] Unable to find the root directory. Create a .mvn directory in the root directory or add the root="true" attribute on the root project's model to identify it. As written in the warning, there are two ways to define the project's root directory: Create a .mvn directory in the root directory. From Maven's perspective, the directory can be empty, but some version control systems do not check in an empty directory. Therefore, placing an empty file inside (or a Maven configuration files ) works around this. Using the .mvn directory is already possible with Maven 3. Set the root attribute in your parent POM to true . The root attribute is a new attribute of model version 4.1.0 and therefore can only be used with Maven 4. Note: That is also the cause, why this topic is listed in the model version 4.1.0 section. Use <subprojects> instead of <modules> In Maven 4 subprojects are no longer called modules, to avoid confusion between Maven modules and Java Modules introduced in Java 9. While the <modules> element is still supported, it was marked as deprecated in model version 4.1.0 and will get removed in a future version. So you should replace it with the new <subprojects> element instead. <!-- Requires model version 4.0.0 (Maven 3, deprecated in model version 4.1.0) --> <modules> <module> moduleA </module> <module> moduleB </module> </modules> <!-- Requires model version 4.1.0 (Maven 4) --> <subprojects> <subproject> moduleA </subproject> <subproject> moduleB </subproject> </subprojects> Automatic versioning in multi subprojects setups Maven 4 contains a lot of improvements for projects which contain subprojects. Those include automatic version detection of the parent and project own dependencies, and automatic detection of parent groupId and artifactId. Using Maven 3 with model version 4.0.0, you need to declare those. While the parent's version always must be hardcoded, you can use the ${project.version} property to declare another subproject as a dependency. Using Maven 4 and model version 4.1.0, those definitions are optional: they are automatically inferred from content on disk. The following example of a pom.xml shows the associated part for a subproject called "subprojectB". This subproject declares its parent and the dependency to "subprojectA", which is also a subproject in the same multi subproject setup. In Maven 3 with model version 4.0.0 such a declaration looks like the following. <project xmlns= "http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0" xmlns:xsi= "http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xsi:schemaLocation= "http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 http://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd" > <modelVersion> 4.0.0 </modelVersion> <artifactId> subprojectB </artifactId> <parent> <!-- The parent groupId and artifactId must be "hardcoded" --> <groupId> demo.maven </groupId> <artifactId> theParentProjecct </artifactId> <!-- The parents' version must be "hardcoded" --> <version> 0.0.1-SNAPSHOT </version> </parent> <dependencies> <dependency> <groupId> demo.maven </groupId> <artifactId> subprojectA </artifactId> <!-- The subproject dependency version declaration can make use of the project.version property--> <version> ${project.version} </version> </dependency> </dependencies> <!-- other declarations --> </project> In Maven 4 and model version 4.1.0, the version declarations and parent coordinates are not needed anymore. <project xmlns= "http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.1.0" xmlns:xsi= "http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xsi:schemaLocation= "http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.1.0 http://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.1.0.xsd" > <modelVersion> 4.1.0 </modelVersion> <artifactId> subprojectB </artifactId> <parent/> <dependencies> <dependency> <groupId> demo.maven </groupId> <artifactId> subprojectA </artifactId> </dependency> </dependencies> <!-- other declarations --> </project> CI-friendly variables without flatten-maven-plugin Maven partially supports CI-friendly variables (like ${revision} ) since version 3.5.0. Thanks to the improved dependency resolution of project own dependencies in multi subprojects setups they are now fully supported if you rely on the automatic versioning as described in the section above. This also means that you don't need the flatten-maven-plugin to install and deploy anymore. Using BOM packaging Maven 4 introduces a dedicated bom packaging type to provide a Bill of Materials BOM POM . This now differentiates between parent POMs and dependency-managing BOM POMs. The new type is only available as a build POM in Model Version 4.1.0 and later, but Maven generates a full Maven 3 compatible consumer POM during the build. The following code snippet shows an example for a BOM POM using the new <packaging> type. <project xmlns= "http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.1.0" xmlns:xsi= "http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xsi:schemaLocation= "http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.1.0 http://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.1.0.xsd" > <modelVersion> 4.1.0 </modelVersion> <groupId> demo.maven </groupId> <artifactId> maven4-example-bom </artifactId> <version> 1.0.0 </version> <packaging> bom </packaging> <dependencyManagement> <dependencies> <dependency> <groupId> dev.some.group </groupId> <artifactId> someArtifact </artifactId> <version> 1.2.3 </version> </dependency> <dependency> <groupId> dev.some.other </groupId> <artifactId> somethingElse </artifactId> <version> 3.1.5 </version> </dependency> </dependencies> </dependencyManagement> </project> Use the new all and each life cycle phases Maven 4 introduces several new lifecycle phases — all , each , before:all , after:all , before:each , and after:each . They give users finer control over plugin execution, particularly in multi-project and concurrent builds. If you want to execute a plugin before/after all or each of your (sub-)projects, consider to use them. New way to declare source directories Maven 3 has two explicitly named XML elements ( <sourceDirectory> and <testSourceDirectory> ) to declare the root directories of source code, as shown below: <project> <build> <sourceDirectory> my-custom-dir/foo </sourceDirectory> <testSourceDirectory> my-custom-dir/bar </testSourceDirectory> </build> </project> Maven 4 introduces the new <sources> element for this. This makes source directory declarations more flexible for future improvements like Java Modules. When migrate to Maven 4, you should use the new element. <project> <build> <sources> <source> <scope> main </scope> <directory> my-custom-dir/foo </directory> </source> <source> <scope> test </scope> <directory> my-custom-dir/bar </directory> </source> </sources> </build> </project>

title: Troubleshooting and required changes if situation applies
text: The following changes are in general not required by all projects, but might apply to yours. Fix plugin misconfigurations There are several misconfigurations in
terms: --fail-on-severity WARN project.rootDirectory session.topDirectory session.rootDirectory executionRootDirectory multiModuleProjectDirectory pre- post- integration-test clean test before after pre-integration-test post-integration-test
body: The following changes are in general not required by all projects, but might apply to yours. Fix plugin misconfigurations There are several misconfigurations in the project's POM declaration that result in warnings when using Maven 3.9. While your build should not throw any warnings at all, the following ones needs to be fixed as they will fail the build in Maven 4. Notes : The plugin configuration guide contains general information, how plugins are correctly declared and configured. For analysing wrong build behavior, it might help to use the new --fail-on-severity parameter, paired with WARN as an argument, to fail your build when a warning occurs. Duplicate plugin declaration A plugin must only be declared once. Defining it multiple times results the following log message. 'build.plugins.plugin.(groupId:artifactId)' must be unique but found duplicate declaration of plugin [plugin-name] ... To fix this, remove the duplicated configuration. Replace removed directory properties Maven 4 introduces new public properties dedicated to point to the root and top directory of (multi-subproject) project. You can now use ${project.rootDirectory} , ${session.topDirectory} , ${session.rootDirectory} when declaring paths. See the Maven Model Builder interpolation reference for more details. At the same time, several (especially internal) properties are deprecated or removed. This includes the following properties: executionRootDirectory multiModuleProjectDirectory Replace plugin bindings to pre- and post- lifecycle phase In Maven 3, integration-test , clean and test lifecycle phases have pre- and post- phases. In Maven 4 those phases are removed in favor of new before: and after: phases, available for all lifecycle phases . Update your plugin executions that bind to a pre-integration-test or post-integration-test phase with the corresponding before:integration-test or after:integration-test phases.

title: Mixins (Maven 4.1)
text: Maven Mixins will provide (in Maven 4.1) a powerful mechanism for sharing common POM configuration across multiple projects without the limitations of tradition
body: Maven Mixins will provide (in Maven 4.1) a powerful mechanism for sharing common POM configuration across multiple projects without the limitations of traditional inheritance. Mixins allow you to compose your project configuration from multiple sources, promoting better code reuse and maintainability.

title: Advanced Features
text: Mixin Composition Order Mixins are applied in the order they are declared. Later mixins can override configuration from earlier mixins: <mixins> <mixin> <groupI
body: Mixin Composition Order Mixins are applied in the order they are declared. Later mixins can override configuration from earlier mixins: <mixins> <mixin> <groupId> com.example.mixins </groupId> <artifactId> base-mixin </artifactId> <version> 1.0.0 </version> </mixin> <mixin> <groupId> com.example.mixins </groupId> <artifactId> override-mixin </artifactId> <version> 1.0.0 </version> </mixin> </mixins> Combining with Inheritance Mixins work alongside traditional POM inheritance. The resolution order is: Parent POM configuration Mixin configurations (in declaration order) Current POM configuration <project> <modelVersion> 4.2.0 </modelVersion> <parent> <groupId> com.example </groupId> <artifactId> parent-pom </artifactId> <version> 1.0.0 </version> </parent> <mixins> <mixin> <groupId> com.example.mixins </groupId> <artifactId> java-mixin </artifactId> <version> 1.0.0 </version> </mixin> </mixins> <artifactId> my-project </artifactId> <!-- Project-specific overrides --> </project> Version Management Like dependencies, mixin versions can be managed centrally: <project> <modelVersion> 4.2.0 </modelVersion> <mixinManagement> <mixins> <mixin> <groupId> com.example.mixins </groupId> <artifactId> java-mixin </artifactId> <version> 1.0.0 </version> </mixin> <mixin> <groupId> com.example.mixins </groupId> <artifactId> testing-mixin </artifactId> <version> 2.0.0 </version> </mixin> </mixins> </mixinManagement> <mixins> <mixin> <groupId> com.example.mixins </groupId> <artifactId> java-mixin </artifactId> <!-- Version inherited from mixinManagement --> </mixin> </mixins> </project>

body: Declaring Mixins Mixins are declared in the <mixins> section of your POM: <project> <modelVersion> 4.2.0 </modelVersion> <groupId> com.example </groupId> <artifactId> my-project </artifactId> <version> 1.0.0 </version> <mixins> <mixin> <groupId> com.example.mixins </groupId> <artifactId> java-mixin </artifactId> <version> 1.0.0 </version> </mixin> <mixin> <groupId> com.example.mixins </groupId> <artifactId> testing-mixin </artifactId> <version> 1.0.0 </version> </mixin> </mixins> <!-- Your project-specific configuration --> </project> Model Version Requirement Mixins require model version 4.2.0 (introduced with Maven 4.1.0) or higher. This new model version was introduced specifically to support the mixins feature while maintaining backward compatibility.

title: Best Practices
text: 1. Keep Mixins Focused Each mixin should have a single, well-defined purpose: ✅ java-17-mixin - Java 17 compilation settings ✅ spring-boot-mixin - Spring Boot c
body: 1. Keep Mixins Focused Each mixin should have a single, well-defined purpose: ✅ java-17-mixin - Java 17 compilation settings ✅ spring-boot-mixin - Spring Boot configuration ✅ testing-mixin - Testing framework setup ❌ everything-mixin - Kitchen sink approach 2. Use Semantic Versioning Version your mixins using semantic versioning to communicate compatibility: 1.0.0 - Initial release 1.1.0 - New features, backward compatible 2.0.0 - Breaking changes 3. Document Your Mixins Include clear documentation in your mixin POMs: <project> <modelVersion> 4.2.0 </modelVersion> <groupId> com.example.mixins </groupId> <artifactId> java-mixin </artifactId> <version> 1.0.0 </version> <packaging> pom </packaging> <name> Java Compilation Mixin </name> <description> Provides standardized Java compilation settings including: - Java 17 source/target compatibility - UTF-8 encoding - Compiler warnings and error handling - Code quality checks </description> <url> https://github.com/example/maven-mixins </url> <!-- Configuration follows --> </project> 4. Test Your Mixins Create test projects that use your mixins to ensure they work correctly: maven-mixins/ ├── java-mixin/ │ └── pom.xml ├── testing-mixin/ │ └── pom.xml └── test-projects/ ├── simple-java-project/ │ └── pom.xml (uses java-mixin) └── spring-boot-project/ └── pom.xml (uses java-mixin + spring-boot-mixin) 5. Organize Mixins in a Dedicated Repository Consider organizing your mixins in a dedicated repository or module: company-maven-mixins/ ├── pom.xml (parent for all mixins) ├── java-mixin/ ├── spring-boot-mixin/ ├── testing-mixin/ ├── quality-mixin/ └── README.md

body: 1. Technology Stack Mixins Create mixins for specific technology stacks: <!-- spring-boot-mixin --> <project> <modelVersion> 4.2.0 </modelVersion> <groupId> com.example.mixins </groupId> <artifactId> spring-boot-mixin </artifactId> <version> 1.0.0 </version> <packaging> pom </packaging> <properties> <spring-boot.version> 3.1.0 </spring-boot.version> </properties> <dependencyManagement> <dependencies> <dependency> <groupId> org.springframework.boot </groupId> <artifactId> spring-boot-dependencies </artifactId> <version> ${spring-boot.version} </version> <type> pom </type> <scope> import </scope> </dependency> </dependencies> </dependencyManagement> <build> <plugins> <plugin> <groupId> org.springframework.boot </groupId> <artifactId> spring-boot-maven-plugin </artifactId> <version> ${spring-boot.version} </version> </plugin> </plugins> </build> </project> 2. Quality Assurance Mixins Standardize code quality tools across projects: <!-- quality-mixin --> <project> <modelVersion> 4.2.0 </modelVersion> <groupId> com.example.mixins </groupId> <artifactId> quality-mixin </artifactId> <version> 1.0.0 </version> <packaging> pom </packaging> <build> <plugins> <plugin> <groupId> org.sonarsource.scanner.maven </groupId> <artifactId> sonar-maven-plugin </artifactId> <version> 3.9.1.2184 </version> </plugin> <plugin> <groupId> com.github.spotbugs </groupId> <artifactId> spotbugs-maven-plugin </artifactId> <version> 4.7.3.0 </version> </plugin> <plugin> <groupId> org.jacoco </groupId> <artifactId> jacoco-maven-plugin </artifactId> <version> 0.8.8 </version> <executions> <execution> <goals> <goal> prepare-agent </goal> </goals> </execution> <execution> <id> report </id> <phase> test </phase> <goals> <goal> report </goal> </goals> </execution> </executions> </plugin> </plugins> </build> </project> 3. Testing Mixins Standardize testing configurations: <!-- testing-mixin --> <project> <modelVersion> 4.2.0 </modelVersion> <groupId> com.example.mixins </groupId> <artifactId> testing-mixin </artifactId> <version> 1.0.0 </version> <packaging> pom </packaging> <properties> <junit.version> 5.9.2 </junit.version> <mockito.version> 5.1.1 </mockito.version> </properties> <dependencyManagement> <dependencies> <dependency> <groupId> org.junit.jupiter </groupId> <artifactId> junit-jupiter </artifactId> <version> ${junit.version} </version> <scope> test </scope> </dependency> <dependency> <groupId> org.mockito </groupId> <artifactId> mockito-core </artifactId> <version> ${mockito.version} </version> <scope> test </scope> </dependency> </dependencies> </dependencyManagement> <build> <plugins> <plugin> <groupId> org.apache.maven.plugins </groupId> <artifactId> maven-surefire-plugin </artifactId> <version> 3.0.0-M9 </version> <configuration> <includes> <include> **/*Test.java </include> <include> **/*Tests.java </include> </includes> </configuration> </plugin> </plugins> </build> </project>

title: Conclusion
text: Maven Mixins provide a powerful and flexible way to share configuration across projects while avoiding the limitations of traditional inheritance. By composing
body: Maven Mixins provide a powerful and flexible way to share configuration across projects while avoiding the limitations of traditional inheritance. By composing your project configuration from focused, reusable mixins, you can: Reduce configuration duplication Improve maintainability Enable better separation of concerns Facilitate standardization across teams and organizations Start small by creating mixins for your most common configuration patterns, and gradually build a library of reusable components that can accelerate your development process.

title: Overview
text: Maven Mixins address several limitations of traditional POM inheritance: Single inheritance limitation : Maven POMs can only inherit from one parent, limiting r
body: Maven Mixins address several limitations of traditional POM inheritance: Single inheritance limitation : Maven POMs can only inherit from one parent, limiting reusability Deep inheritance hierarchies : Complex inheritance chains can be difficult to understand and maintain Configuration duplication : Common configurations often need to be duplicated across projects Tight coupling : Changes to parent POMs can have unintended effects on child projects Mixins solve these problems by allowing you to include configuration from multiple sources in a composable way.

title: What's new in Maven 4
text: title: What's new in Maven 4? author: Matthias Bünger Note : This article will continuously be updated at least until Maven 4.0.0 is released. Maven is over 20
body: title: What's new in Maven 4? author: Matthias Bünger Note : This article will continuously be updated at least until Maven 4.0.0 is released. Maven is over 20 years old, and is the most widely used build tool in the Java world. Throughout the years, Maven has maintained backward compatibility, especially of its POM file with Model version 4.0.0. The POM file fulfills two needs. First, the POM holds all the information and configuration, which are needed to build the artifact. After the artifact is created, this build information is not relevant anymore. Second, the POM also contains information, for example dependencies, which are needed by projects which depend on the artifact. These dependent projects are called the "consumers". This made Maven more than a tool; it became a whole ecosystem with many dependencies on the POM, especially the Maven Central repository, other build tools, and IDEs. Thus, any change in the POM's schema forces each participant of the ecosystem to either adopt the change or drop support. Thus, the Maven POM syntax became fixed, unable to change. "With the Maven build schema preserved in amber, we can’t evolve much: we’ll stay forever with Maven 3 minor releases, unable to implement improvements that we imagine will require seriously updating the POM schema…" — Hervé Boutemy (in Javaadvent 2021) In order for Maven to evolve, it's necessary to separate the information needed for the build from the information needed by the consumers, but without breaking the ecosystem. Maven 4 prepares for this and more. This article presents and explains major changes brought by Maven 4, grouped into several topics.

title: Improvements for subprojects
text: Automatic versioning (POM inference) Maven 4 finally ships one of the oldest improvement requests - automatic parent versioning ( MNG-624 , created in July 2005
terms: <version> <groupId> <artifactId> <parent> pom.xml <relativePath> relativePath> parent> <parent <subprojects> <modules> pom revision mvn verify Drevision maven.config --resume-from <nameOfTheFailingSubproject> --also-make <nameOfTheDependentSubproject> clean install --resume -r deployAtEnd true
body: Automatic versioning (POM inference) Maven 4 finally ships one of the oldest improvement requests - automatic parent versioning ( MNG-624 , created in July 2005 and originally planned for Maven 2)! As expected, it's no longer required to define the parent versions in each subproject when using the new model version 4.1.0. This also extends to dependencies of project's own subprojects and reduces the need to update POM files for new versions even more. Parent inference When using model version 4.1.0, you can omit the <version> , <groupId> , and <artifactId> elements from <parent> by using a relative path. Maven will automatically infer these values by looking for a pom.xml file in the specified directory. You can use either of these forms: <parent><relativePath>..</relativePath></parent> - explicitly specify the relative path to the parent directory or even <parent/> - shorthand form that defaults to looking in the parent directory ( .. ) This makes it easier to maintain multi-project builds without duplicating <version> and coordinate information. Subprojects discovery Maven 4 can also automatically discover subprojects in subdirectories without requiring them to be explicitly listed in the <subprojects> (or deprecated <modules> ) section. This reduces boilerplate in your POM files (in source control) and makes it easier to add new subprojects to your build. Subprojects are automatically discovered when: The parent POM has pom packaging No <subprojects> or <modules> section is explicitly defined Direct subdirectories contain a pom.xml file When these conditions are met, Maven will automatically add all subdirectories with a pom.xml file to the list of subprojects to build. Example The following code snippet shows the parent and dependency definition without the version tag. <project xmlns= "http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.1.0" xmlns:xsi= "http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xsi:schemaLocation= "http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.1.0 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.1.0.xsd" > <parent> <groupId> my.parents.groupId </groupId> <artifactId> my.parents.artifactId </artifactId> </parent> <artifactId> myOwnSubprojectArtifactId </artifactId> <dependencies> <dependency> <groupId> the.dependent.subproject.groupId </groupId> <artifactId> the.dependent.subproject.artifactId </artifactId> </dependency> </dependencies> </project> Full support of CI-friendly variables Maven 3.5.0 introduced partial support for CI-friendly variables, like ${revision} , in your POM files. However, this still required using the Flatten Maven Plugin for full functionality. Since Maven 4, no additional plugin is needed; full built-in support is provided. You can now use any variable as a version in your configuration, not just predefined ones. Example <groupId> my.groupId </groupId> <artifactId> my.artifactId </artifactId> <version> ${revision} </version> Variables must be defined at build time using one of the following methods: Maven properties defined on the command line, for example mvn verify -Drevision=4.0.1 Maven properties defined in a maven.config file in the .mvn directory Maven properties defined in the root POM or parent POM This flexibility allows you to use any variable name you prefer, making it easier to integrate Maven with your CI/CD pipelines and build automation systems. Maven maintainer Karl Heinz Marbaise shows a larger example in his article "Maven 4 - Part I - Easier Versions" (2024) . Reactor improvements and fixes Building a project with multiple subprojects can cause confusion in Maven 3. When the build of subproject B, which requires subproject A, is failing for whatever reason, Maven 3 is telling the user to fix the error and then resume the build with --resume-from :<nameOfTheFailingSubproject> . But doing this instantly fails the build again, because the required subproject A couldn't be found (as it was not rebuilt). Using --also-make :<nameOfTheDependentSubproject> was no help in the past as it was ignored due to the long-standing bug MNG-6863 - which is finally fixed with Maven 4! Recommendation: Do not use mvn clean install for your regular builds. Instead, use mvn verify ! To improve usability when resuming a failed build, you can now use --resume or its short parameter -r to resume a build from the subproject that last failed. So you don't have to manually pass the name of the failed subproject as the starting point to resume from. The reactor is now also aware of successfully built subprojects when the overall build failed and will skip rebuilding those if you resume the build. With Maven 4, it's also aware of subfolder builds MNG-6118 , which becomes pretty handy when you only want to execute tools (for example Jetty) on/with certain subprojects, but not on every subproject. See Maven maintainer Maarten Mulders's article "What's New in Maven 4" (2020) for a small example. Further improvements Further improvements to subprojects will also improve daily work with them: Thanks to MNG-6754 , all subprojects will now have consistent SNAPSHOT timestamps in their packaged archives in local/remote repositories, while in Maven 3, each subproject had a different one. This should make it easier to identify the archives that belong together. When using Maven 3, deploying a project with multiple subprojects could end up in a situation where successfully built subprojects were deployed to the (local or remote) repository, but failed subprojects were not. This was finally changed in Maven 4 to what most users expect: Only deploy when all subprojects are built successfully. This means that the default value of the deployAtEnd parameter is now true .
