title: Maven plugins, security, and tools
text: Maven plugins As mentioned above, Maven 4 contains significant code and API updates, resulting in breaking changes for (very) old Maven 2 plugins that have not
terms: Dmaven.plugin.validation verbose mvnenc decrypt mvn mvnd mvnsh
body: Maven plugins As mentioned above, Maven 4 contains significant code and API updates, resulting in breaking changes for (very) old Maven 2 plugins that have not been updated to use the recommended Maven 3 APIs and other cleanup . You can enable verbose plugin validation by passing the following argument to your build: -Dmaven.plugin.validation=verbose (see detailed plugin validation guide ). You should also only rely on the official Maven BOMs when developing plugins. If a plugin still relies on long-deprecated and now removed Plexus dependency injection, it will no longer work. It needs to be updated to use JSR-330 - see Maven & JSR-330 for further information. Advice : If you are maintaining a Maven plugin, you should test it with Maven 3.9.x. Pay close attention to upcoming warnings and update the plugin accordingly. Maven 4 is expected to be able to run any Maven 3 plugin that has been updated to Maven 3 best practices (instead of using Maven 3's ability to run Maven 2 plugins and other old APIs...). Major changes regarding plugins include a proper immutable plugin model together with a revised plugin API for Maven 4. But this new Maven 4 API is still in experimental phase in Maven 4.0.0: do not yet try to use it unless you precisely know what you are doing (like Maven Compiler Plugin 4.x for Java Modules). Improved encryption Security is important, and storing unencrypted passwords is bad practice. Maven 3's password encryption had several serious issues and could more accurately be called "password obfuscation". Maven 4 instead has a completely redone encryption system, based on Maven Encryption ( mvnenc ) - a standalone CLI tool. As of now, it provides functionally equivalent operations as Maven 3 (see "Maven: Password Encryption" ) but adds improvements like a decrypt functionality and supports external vaults. The documentation of the new encryption can be found in "Password Encryption (Maven 4)" . A broad overview of the problems in Maven 3 and the solution in Maven 4 can be found in the article "Handling sensitive data in Maven" by Maven maintainer Tamás Cservenák. Maven Resolver The Maven Artifact Resolver is a library for working with artifact repositories and dependency resolution. Maven 4 includes the new 2.0 release of this library, which contains more than 150 fixes, upgrades, and improvements, for example, a Java native HTTP-Client - thanks to raising the Java version requirement to JDK 17! Another major difference compared to Maven 3 is that in the new major version, the resolver is hidden behind the new Maven API and is no longer used directly by plugins. Maven Shell Each time you run an mvn command, the entire process chain is executed: booting Java, starting Maven, loading the configuration, performing the task, tearing down, and exiting — every single time . To improve performance and reduce build times, you can use the Maven Daemon ( mvnd ), which manages a pool of resident Maven processes. With Maven 4, you can also take advantage of the newly defined " Maven Shell " ( mvnsh ), which keeps a single Maven process running for as long as the shell remains open. Maven Upgrade Tool To upgrade from Maven 3 to Maven 4, you can use the Maven Upgrade Tool . This tool helps automate the migration process by analyzing your project and making necessary adjustments to ensure compatibility with Maven 4. The Maven Upgrade Tool can be used to: Update your POM files to use the new model version 4.1.0 (if desired) Identify deprecated features and suggest replacements Migrate from deprecated plugin configurations to their modern equivalents Validate that your project is ready for Maven 4 Refer to Maven Upgrade Tool for more information on usage and the upgrade process in general.

title: POM Changes
text: Consumer POM Maven 4 can generate a stripped down consumer POM that removes build information not needed by consumers, and deploys this to the remote repository
terms: pom.xml maven.consumer.pom.flatten true session.rootDirectory mvn maven-user.properties http maven.apache.org POM src <modules> <subprojects> multi-project setup single-project <dependency> jar classpath-jar modular-jar processor classpath-processor modular-processor classpath- modular- bom <exclusions> <classifier> maven.config jvm.config root
body: Consumer POM Maven 4 can generate a stripped down consumer POM that removes build information not needed by consumers, and deploys this to the remote repository. It does not deploy the pom.xml used to build the project. The consumer POM is a flattened version of the build POM, meaning: It contains no parent POM references (all inherited elements are resolved and included directly) BOM imports are flattened into the dependency list Only transitive dependencies are kept (compile and runtime scopes) Managed dependencies are kept only if they are actually used by the project This flattening ensures that consumers of your artifact have all the information they need without requiring access to parent POMs or understanding the internal structure of your multi-project build. The flatten feature is disabled by default to avoid unexpected behavior and better control of listing (transitive) dependencies in the consumer POM. To publish a flattened consumer POM instead of the full build POM, the user property maven.consumer.pom.flatten must be set to true . User properties can be controlled using ${session.rootDirectory}/.mvn/maven-user.properties for a per-reactor configuration. Model version 4.1.0 Maven 4 updates the POM version to 4.1.0 which defines the namespace http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.1.0 . Version 4.1.0 adds some new elements and attributes, while others are marked as deprecated. To not break the ecosystem, this version is only available for the build POM (stored in source control), while the consumer POM (available in remote repositories like Maven Central) will still use version 4.0.0. Maven generates the consumer POM during the build from the build POM. Note : Maven 4 will continue to build your Maven 3's model version 4.0.0 project. There is no need to update your (build) POMs to 4.1.0 if you don't need to use the new features. Modules are now subprojects A Maven project is any Java project built with Maven. The top level directory of a Maven project contains at least the source folder src and the project's POM file pom.xml . A Maven project may have other Maven projects within subdirectories, each with its own pom.xml file. Each project within a subdirectory is called a "subproject". Example: Project A contains a subdirectory which contains its own POM file for project B. We say that B is a subproject of A. However, Maven does not build subprojects unless they are linked from the root POM file. In the past this was done by listing each subproject in the <modules> section of the parent's POM. Projects which have at least one subproject are called "multi-module projects", while those which do not have any subprojects are called "single module projects". Since the introduction of the Java Platform Module System in Java 9, the term "module" has raised additional confusion inside the Maven community. Maven 4 gets rid of this by renaming modules to projects and submodules to subprojects. Model version 4.1.0 contains a new <subprojects> element analogous to the now deprecated, but still usable, <modules> element. Note : Use the terms multi-project setup and single-project setup to differentiate between a Maven project with or without subprojects. New artifact types Maven 4 introduces new types of artifacts. The types listed below can be used in <dependency> declarations of JAR files. The jar type existed in Maven 3 and is still the default in Maven 4. The other types are new: jar : for a JAR file that can be placed either on the class path or on the module path. classpath-jar : for a JAR file that is unconditionally placed on the class path. modular-jar : for a JAR file that is unconditionally placed on the module path. processor : for a JAR file that can be placed either on the annotation processor class path or module path. classpath-processor : for a JAR file to unconditionally place on the annotation processor class path. modular-processor : for a JAR file to unconditionally place on the annotation processor module path. The jar and processor types use heuristic rules for deciding where to place the JAR file, but the result is not always what the developer wants. The types with classpath- or modular- prefix give control to the developer. Limitation: As of October 2025, only Maven Compiler Plugin (version 4.0.0-beta-3 and newer) complies with the new types. Other plugins will be updated progressively. New packaging type: bom Maven 4 introduces a dedicated bom packaging type to provide a Bill of Materials BOM POM . This now differentiates between parent POMs and dependency-managing BOMs. The new type is only available as a build POM in Model Version 4.1.0 and later, but Maven generates a full Maven 3 compatible consumer POM during the build. For an example, see the link above or the live coding by Maven maintainer Karl Heinz Marbaise at IntelliJ IDEA Conf 2024 . Note : With Maven 4, it's also possible to exclude dependencies that are declared by BOMs using the existing <exclusions> element. Also note that in Maven 4 (model version 4.1.0 and later), importing BOMs with a classifier is possible by using the standard <classifier> element on the import dependency: <dependencyManagement> <dependencies> <dependency> <groupId> org.example </groupId> <artifactId> example </artifactId> <version> 1.0.0 </version> <type> pom </type> <classifier> bom </classifier> <scope> import </scope> </dependency> </dependencies> </dependencyManagement> Classified BOM artifacts are produced by attaching an additional POM artifact with a classifier (for example via a BOM-building plugin). Consumers import that artifact with the standard <classifier> element as shown above. Therefore, the Maven team suggests that project BOMs should be published as classified artifacts when appropriate. This means that an imported BOM must not come from the same reactor as the current build but be available outside the project before the build. In other words: you should only import external BOMs. That's why Maven 4.0 will show a warning if a BOM comes from the same reactor. In the future, this will most probably be changed to make the build fail. Comparing build POM and consumer POM The following table shows a rough comparison of which content is available in which POM type when using Maven 4. Notes : The column "consumer POM" does not apply to artifacts that are of type "pom", because "pom"-artifacts are designed to contain build information, for example plugin configuration! Some of the build-related content which is (as of now) still available in the consumer POM might be available only in the build POM in the future. Content Build POM Consumer POM Model version 4.1.0 4.0.0 3rd party dependency information ✅ ✅ POM properties ✅ ❌ Plugin configuration ✅ ❌ Repository information ✅ ✅ Project information / environment settings ✅ ✅ Deployment to remote repository ✅ ✅ Warning : There are rare situations where Maven 4 will produce a consumer POM based on version 4.1.0, for example when condition-based profiles (see below) can't be transformed to version 4.0.0. Maven will show a warning in such situations. Declaring the root directory and directory properties Every time Maven executes a build, it has to determine the project's root to identify things like the parent project, directory information, and so on. To "help" Maven find the root folder, you can create a .mvn folder in your root directory. This folder is intended to contain project-specific configuration to run Maven, for example a maven.config or jvm.config file, and therefore was also considered as the root folder. With Maven 4, there is a second option to clearly define the root folder. Model version 4.1.0, usable for the build POM, adds a boolean attribute called root in the <project> element. When this attribute is set to true (default is false), the directory of this POM file is considered the root directory. Another pain point in relation to the root directory is that until Maven 4, there was no official property to make use of the root folder in your POM files, for example when you want to define the path to a checkstyle-suppressions.xml file for the checkstyle plugin. Maven 4 now provides official properties to reference the root directory in your POM configuration. The following table shows the official properties. Property Scope Definition Always ${project.rootDirectory} Project .mvn folder or root attribute in pom No ${session.topDirectory} Session Current directory or --file argument Yes ${session.rootDirectory} Session .mvn folder or root attribute in pom for the topDirectory project No As you can see, these properties differentiate by their scope, where project is always related to the Maven project's definition (you could interpret this as the POM files) and session is the actual execution of a Maven build and is the current working directory. The rootDirectory can only contain a value when either a .mvn directory is defined or the root attribute is set to true. However, if defined, it should always have the same value for a given project, whereas the value of the topDirectory property can change depending on the execution point. Keep in mind that the root directory of the whole project (when considering multiple subprojects) is different from each subproject's own base directory, which is accessible via the ${basedir} property for use in POM files and will always have a value. Note: In the past, some people "hacked" workarounds for the rootDirectory properties, mostly by using internal properties. Starting with Maven 4 those properties were removed or marked as deprecated. See JIRA issue MNG-7038 and the related Pull Request for MNG-7038 for more information. New way to declare source directories Maven 3 has two explicitly named XML elements ( <sourceDirectory> and <testSourceDirectory> ) to declare the root directories of source code, as shown below: <project> <build> <sourceDirectory> my-custom-dir/foo </sourceDirectory> <testSourceDirectory> my-custom-dir/bar </testSourceDirectory> </build> </project> Maven 4 introduces the new <sources> element for this. Multiple <source> elements can be repeated, thus allowing multiple source directories without the need to resort to external plugins (like Build Helper Maven Plugin ). It also provides a unified way to declare include/exclude filters, makes easier to set up projects targeting multi Java releases, and enables Java module source hierarchy. The documentation of the Maven Compiler Plugin gives some examples and more details. <project> <build> <sources> <source> <scope> main </scope> <directory> my-custom-dir/foo </directory> </source> <source> <scope> test </scope> <directory> my-custom-dir/bar </directory> </source> </sources> </build> </project> Alternate POM syntaxes While the syntax for the 4.0.0 consumer POM is set in stone, the build POM should be able to evolve. This includes allowing the use of alternate syntaxes to XML by having Maven 4 provide a ModelParser SPI ( MNG-7836 ), which can be implemented as a core extension and allow a custom syntax. One of the first projects that uses this feature is the Apache Maven Hocon Extension .

title: Required Java version
text: Maven 4 requires Java 17. This allows Maven (and its maintainers) to make use of newer language features and improvements. Important note : Java 17 is only need
body: Maven 4 requires Java 17. This allows Maven (and its maintainers) to make use of newer language features and improvements. Important note : Java 17 is only needed to run Maven ! You can still compile against older Java versions using the same compiler plugin configuration as before. If you need to compile against or use another JDK, see the Guide to Using Toolchains (or the article Introduction to Maven Toolchains by Maven maintainer Maarten Mulders).

title: Workflow, lifecycle and runtime changes
text: Application maintenance As with every major update, extensive application maintenance has occurred, including significant code, API, and dependencies updates. F
terms: pom. --fail-on-severity -fos WARN <condition> <activation> compile compile-only ready deploy install -b concurrent mvn verify before after integration-test pre- post- process-resources pre-compile post-clean clean all each validate test
body: Application maintenance As with every major update, extensive application maintenance has occurred, including significant code, API, and dependencies updates. For example, the "Plexus Containers" dependency injection was removed - after being deprecated since Maven 3.2 (2010)! Code updates include not only newer Java language features but also changes to make maintenance easier and less time-consuming. This also includes removing features that either should never have worked or were only kept for backward compatibility in Maven 3, for example using ${pom.*} expressions. Maven's own Super POM was also upgraded, which declares new default versions of Maven's core plugins. Note : Due to upgrading the default versions of Maven plugins, your build might behave differently than before, even if you didn't purposely change anything. To avoid this situation, always define fixed versions of all the plugins you use. By doing this, you are in control of your build. Maven 4 will issue a warning if you rely on default versions defined in Maven's Super POM. "Fail on severity" parameter Maven 4 introduces a "fail on severity" build parameter, which breaks the build when the severity of at least one log message matches the given argument. The parameter can either be used by its full name ( --fail-on-severity ) or as a short handle ( -fos ). The parameter is followed by an argument specifying a log level severity, for example, WARN . Improvements to profiles Trying to use a nonexistent profile in a build causes the build to fail, as the following command line snippet shows: > mvn compile -Pnonexistent [ERROR] The requested profiles [nonexistent] could not be activated or deactivated because they do not exist. Maven 4 introduces the possibility to use profiles only when they exist, like Maven 3. To do so, the ? argument was added to the profile parameter. When using this, the build won't break if a profile does not exist. Instead, an information message will be printed twice (at the start and end). See the following snippet for an example: > mvn compile -P?nonexistent [INFO] The requested optional profiles [nonexistent] could not be activated or deactivated because they do not exist. [...] [INFO] BUILD SUCCESS [INFO] ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- [INFO] Total time: 0.746 s [INFO] Finished at: 2024-12-14T13:24:15+01:00 [INFO] ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- [INFO] The requested optional profiles [nonexistent] could not be activated or deactivated because they do not exist. Condition-based profile activation Maven 4 introduces more flexible ways to activate profiles by providing condition-based activation through the new <condition> element in the <activation> section. This allows you to use expressions to determine when a profile should be activated, providing much more control than the traditional property-based or OS-based activation. For example, you can now activate profiles based on complex conditions like: Checking if a file exists or doesn't exist Comparing property values Combining multiple conditions with logical operators See MNG-8286 for more information about supported functions and the complete syntax for condition-based activation. Lifecycle changes Lifecycle changed from graph to tree In Maven 3 the lifecycle is an ordered list containing all phases. This changed with Maven 4, where the lifecycle is defined as a tree of phases. This allows for more fine-grained execution of dependent phases. For example, the compile phase must execute after compile-only project dependencies have reached the ready phase. Maven 4 also allows to skip phases (in comparison to the old graph). For example, it's possible to deploy an artifact without install ing it to the user repository. For compatibility, the execution behavior is not really changed by default compared to Maven 3. In order to actually leverage the new tree-based lifecycle, the user has to enable the concurrent builder using -b concurrent . Running with the concurrent builder will allow finer grained dependency instead of the usual Maven 3 per-project dependency. With the usual builders and run mvn verify , a project will run up to the verify phase, before a dependent project can start being built, whereas the concurrent builder will allow a dependant project to be built as soon as the dependencies are at the ready phase. Before- and after-phases, ordering of executions Every lifecycle phase now has a before: and an after: phase, allowing plugins to bind themselves to those. For example, if you want to set up test data before running your integration tests, you could execute tasks during the before:integration-test phase. If this is not enough, perhaps because you want to do multiple things inside the same phase, you can order each execution inside a phase by using square brackets with an integer at the end of the phase name. Example before:integration-test[100] before:integration-test[200] Warning : The conceptual pre-* and post-* phases, which were only available for selected phases and had inconsistent naming, are deprecated. They only act as aliases now and might be removed in the future. Don't use them! This is especially important when binding a plugin to a post-* phase of a lifecycle phase because the corresponding pre-* phase of the desired phase doesn't exist — for example, binding to the process-resources phase due to the absence of a pre-compile phase. Behavioral change: phase execution scope Maven 4 introduces a behavioral change in how phases are executed. For a given major phase, Maven 4 will always execute both ( before: and after: ) minor phases of it. This differs from Maven 3 where the post-* (now after: ) phase is only executed if either the next major phase of the lifecycle is executed or the post-* phase is explicitly called. The following example shows that this change might affect existing builds. Given the following plugin configuration, where a plugin is bound to the post-clean phase. <plugin> <groupId> org.example </groupId> <artifactId> some-plugin </artifactId> <executions> <execution> <!-- In Maven 3: Does NOT run when executing 'mvn clean', only with `mvn post-clean` --> <!-- In Maven 4: DOES run when executing 'mvn clean' --> <phase> post-clean </phase> <goals> <goal> cleanup </goal> </goals> </execution> </executions> </plugin> Running mvn clean using Maven 3 would NOT execute the plugin, because the build execution stops at the main phase, not executing it post- phase. To execute the plugin in Maven 3, the user has to explicitly run mvn post-clean as a build goal. In Maven 4 running mvn clean will also execute the plugin, as both before: and after: phases are always executed and the post- phase is now an alias for after: . All- and each-phases Maven 4 introduces several new lifecycle phases — all , each , before:all , after:all , before:each , and after:each — that give users finer control over plugin execution, particularly in multi-project and concurrent builds. Both the all and each phases are executed for every project and subproject, but their scope differs: The each phase wraps the standard lifecycle phases ( validate , compile , test , etc.) of a single project or subproject. It's used to define behavior that should occur around the build of an individual subproject. The all phase encompasses the entire build of a project, including its each phase and the all phases of its child subprojects. It is ideal for logic that should run once per project, while still covering the entire subproject hierarchy. To make this model more intuitive — especially for users familiar with testing frameworks — Maven 4 also introduces the following hook phases: before:all runs before any other phase in the current project. In a multi-project build, the parent project's before:all is executed before any phases of its subprojects. after:all is executed at the very end of a project’s build. In a multi-project build, the after:all phases of the subprojects run before that of the parent. before:each is executed before every standard phase in a project’s lifecycle, while after:each runs after each phase. These are especially useful for applying consistent setup and teardown logic around every phase. Together, these new phases provide a powerful and intuitive structure for defining and customizing build behavior in complex Maven projects.

title: Aggregation and inheritance
text: How a parent POM passes configuration down, how an aggregator builds modules together, and how the reactor decides the order.
keywords: multi-project monorepo submodule subproject parent POM child POM super POM build order consumer POM build POM cyclic reference Non-resolvable parent POM Unable to find the root directory Gradle settings include
terms: <parent> <relativePath> <modules> <module> <subprojects> pom packaging reactor effective POM help:effective-pom .mvn
body: A multi-module project rests on two separate relationships between POMs. Inheritance lets one POM take its configuration from another: the child names its parent. Aggregation lets one POM build other projects along with itself: the aggregator names its modules. In most projects one POM at the top does both, which is why the two are easy to mix up. They point in opposite directions, though, and each works without the other.

title: Aggregation: an aggregator names its modules
text: An aggregator is a POM with pom packaging and a list of modules. Each <module> is the path from the aggregator's directory to a module's directory or POM file,
body: An aggregator is a POM with pom packaging and a list of modules. Each <module> is the path from the aggregator's directory to a module's directory or POM file, usually the directory name. pom.xml <packaging> pom </packaging> <modules> <module> api </module> <module> core </module> <module> app </module> </modules> When you run Maven on the aggregator, it runs the same command on every module in one build. That is all aggregation does. The aggregator passes no configuration to its modules, and a module does not know which aggregator lists it. Maven 4: The element is called <subprojects> , with one <subproject> per directory, in POMs with model version 4.1.0. <modules> still works there, but Maven reports it as a deprecated element and suggests <subprojects> . When a 4.1.0 POM with pom packaging lists neither, Maven 4 takes every direct subdirectory that has a pom.xml as a subproject.

title: Inheritance: a child names its parent
text: A POM with a <parent> element starts from the parent's configuration and adds its own on top. The parent is a POM like any other, with pom packaging, because it
terms: <parent> pom groupId version artifactId <dependencies> <dependencyManagement> <pluginManagement> <description> <url> <licenses> <developers> <scm> combine.children combine.self name packaging jar <modules> <profiles> https example.com shop url> core mvn help effective-pom -pl
body: A POM with a <parent> element starts from the parent's configuration and adds its own on top. The parent is a POM like any other, with pom packaging, because it produces no jar of its own. core/pom.xml <parent> <groupId> com.example.shop </groupId> <artifactId> shop </artifactId> <version> 1.0-SNAPSHOT </version> </parent> <artifactId> core </artifactId> The child inherits the groupId and version , so it only needs an artifactId . It also inherits properties, <dependencies> , <dependencyManagement> , the build configuration with its plugins and <pluginManagement> , repositories, and descriptive elements such as <description> , <url> , <licenses> , <developers> and <scm> . Lists are merged: the child's dependencies are added to the parent's, and a plugin execution with the same id as one in the parent is merged with it. For plugin configuration you can change how the merge works with combine.children and combine.self , described in the POM reference . Some elements belong to one project only and are not inherited: artifactId and name packaging : a child of a pom parent is a jar unless it says otherwise <modules> : a child does not build its parent's modules <profiles> : the profiles themselves stay in the parent, but what an active parent profile sets, such as a property, does reach the child URLs, including those in <scm> , are inherited with the child's artifactId appended: a parent with <url>https://example.com/shop</url> gives core the URL https://example.com/shop/core . Inheritance is recursive. A parent can have a parent of its own, and at the top of every chain sits the Super POM , built into Maven, which supplies Maven Central as repository and the default directory layout. The result of merging the whole chain is the effective POM, the configuration Maven really builds with. To see it for one module, run this in the root directory: mvn help:effective-pom -pl core

title: Modules see each other's output
text: Within one build, a module that depends on another module gets that module's output from the build itself: its compiled classes, or its jar once it is packaged.
body: Within one build, a module that depends on another module gets that module's output from the build itself: its compiled classes, or its jar once it is packaged. Nothing has to be installed first. That only holds for the modules in the build. When you build one module on its own, Maven 3 looks for the other modules in the local repository, as it would for any dependency, and fails when they were never installed. Build part of a multi-module project shows how to select modules so that what they need is in the build. Maven 4: When Maven 4 packages a subproject, it keeps a copy of the jar in .mvn/target/project-local-repo in the root directory. A later build that leaves that subproject out takes the jar from there before it looks in the local repository. mvn clean removes the copy.

title: One POM or two
text: Usually the root POM is both: the modules name it as their parent, and it lists them as modules. One file then holds the shared configuration and the list of wh
terms: mvn verify parent pom.xml <relativePath> relativePath> lib app
body: Usually the root POM is both: the modules name it as their parent, and it lists them as modules. One file then holds the shared configuration and the list of what to build, and mvn verify in the root directory builds everything. The two roles can be split. A project can keep its shared configuration in parent/pom.xml , inherited by every module through <relativePath>../parent/pom.xml</relativePath> , and have a root POM that only lists parent , lib and app as modules. That root is then an aggregator that nothing inherits from. The other way round is common as well: a company parent POM, inherited by hundreds of projects that are each built on their own, aggregates none of them.

title: The reactor orders the build
text: The part of Maven that builds several projects together is called the reactor. It collects the projects from the aggregator and its modules, recursively, sorts
terms: <dependencyManagement> <pluginManagement> <modules> app core api The projects in the reactor contain a cyclic reference
body: The part of Maven that builds several projects together is called the reactor. It collects the projects from the aggregator and its modules, recursively, sorts them so that every project comes after the projects it needs, and then builds them one by one. A project comes after: the modules it has as a dependency, its parent, when the parent is part of the build, modules it uses as a plugin, as a plugin's dependency or as a build extension. Only those relationships count. An entry in <dependencyManagement> or <pluginManagement> that names another module does not change the order. Where no relationship decides, the order of the <modules> list does. So the order in which you list modules does not matter for correctness: with the modules listed as app , core , api , where app depends on core and core on api , the reactor still prints: [INFO] Reactor Build Order: [INFO] [INFO] shop [pom] [INFO] api [jar] [INFO] core [jar] [INFO] app [jar] The parent comes first because every module inherits from it. An aggregator that is not also the parent has no relationship with its modules, and the reactor may build it last. Two modules that need each other, directly or through others, cannot be ordered. Maven stops before building with The projects in the reactor contain a cyclic reference and names the chain.

title: The root directory and the POM that is published
text: Maven 4: Maven 4 needs to know the root directory of the project. It takes the nearest directory upwards with a .mvn subdirectory, or the directory of a POM wit
terms: mvn root true <project> pom <modules> <subprojects> <parent> build app-1.0-SNAPSHOT-build.pom
body: Maven 4: Maven 4 needs to know the root directory of the project. It takes the nearest directory upwards with a .mvn subdirectory, or the directory of a POM with root="true" on its <project> element (model version 4.1.0). When it finds neither, it warns Unable to find the root directory. Create a .mvn directory in the root directory or add the root="true" attribute on the root project's model to identify it. Maven 3 accepts an empty .mvn directory as well. Maven 4: The POM in your source tree is the build POM. Maven 4 installs and deploys a second POM next to it, the consumer POM, as the .pom file other projects read. It uses model version 4.0.0, so Maven 3 and other tools can read it, with versions that Maven 4 inferred filled in and without <modules> or <subprojects> . By default it keeps the <parent> reference. The build POM is installed and deployed too, with the classifier build , for example app-1.0-SNAPSHOT-build.pom . See What's new in Maven 4 .

title: Where Maven finds the parent
text: Maven looks for the parent in three places, in this order: The POM at <relativePath> , which defaults to ../pom.xml . Maven uses it only if its coordinates matc
body: Maven looks for the parent in three places, in this order: The POM at <relativePath> , which defaults to ../pom.xml . Maven uses it only if its coordinates match those in <parent> . The local repository. The remote repositories. So a parent one directory up needs no <relativePath> . A parent elsewhere needs one, or Maven passes over it and looks in the repositories: lib/pom.xml <parent> <groupId> com.example </groupId> <artifactId> parent </artifactId> <version> 1.0-SNAPSHOT </version> <relativePath> ../parent/pom.xml </relativePath> </parent> Without it, Maven finds another POM at ../pom.xml , or none, and when the parent was never installed the build fails with Non-resolvable parent POM . An empty <relativePath/> tells Maven to skip the file system and take the parent from a repository, which is what you want for a parent from outside the project, such as an organisation-wide parent POM. Maven 4: Maven 4 also finds the parent among the projects of the current build, so a parent that is part of the build is found even when <relativePath> does not point at it. And it can fill in the parent for you: an empty <parent/> means the POM in the directory above, and Maven reads the group id, artifact id and version from that file.

body: Build part of a project when you changed one module and do not want to wait for all of them, or when a build failed halfway. You run these commands in the root directory and select modules with options; Reactor options lists every option and the ways to name a module. The examples use a project shop with the modules api , core and app , where app depends on core and core on api .

body: Add -am (also make) to build the selected module together with every module it depends on, directly or indirectly: mvn verify -pl app -am [INFO] Reactor Summary for shop 1.0-SNAPSHOT: [INFO] [INFO] shop ............................................... SUCCESS [ 0.001 s] [INFO] api ................................................ SUCCESS [ 0.546 s] [INFO] core ............................................... SUCCESS [ 0.014 s] [INFO] app ................................................ SUCCESS [ 0.010 s] [INFO] ------------------------------------------------------------------------ [INFO] BUILD SUCCESS The parent shop is built too, because app inherits from it. None of the project's own modules has to come from the local repository, which makes this the safe way to build one module.

SUCCESS [ 0.586 s] [INFO] app ................................................ SUCCESS [ 0.017 s] [INFO] ------------------------------------------------------------------------ [INFO] BUILD SUCCESS -amd does not add the modules core needs, so api still comes from the local repository. Use both options, -pl core -am -amd , to build core , what it needs and what uses it.

title: Build from a module's directory
text: Running Maven in a module's directory builds that module alone, like -pl , and needs the other modules installed: cd app mvn verify Maven 4: Maven 4 knows the w

body: Running Maven in a module's directory builds that module alone, like -pl , and needs the other modules installed: cd app mvn verify Maven 4: Maven 4 knows the whole project when you start in a subproject's directory. mvn verify -am in app builds shop , api , core and app , and mvn verify -amd in api builds api , core and app . Maven 3 ignores the rest of the project and builds only the module in the current directory.

page: Build part of a multi-module project
title: Build one module
text: Select the module with -pl , followed by its directory: mvn verify -pl core Maven builds core and nothing else. The modules core depends on are not part of this

body: Select the module with -pl , followed by its directory: mvn verify -pl core Maven builds core and nothing else. The modules core depends on are not part of this build, so Maven takes them from the local repository, like any other dependency. If you have never installed them, the build stops: [ERROR] Failed to execute goal on project core: Could not resolve dependencies for project com.example.shop:core:jar:1.0-SNAPSHOT Either install the whole project once with mvn install in the root directory, so that -pl finds the other modules in the local repository, or build the modules it needs along with it, as in the next section. An installed module stays at the version you installed until you install it again. Maven 4: When Maven 4 packages a subproject, it keeps a copy of the jar in .mvn/target/project-local-repo in the root directory, and uses that copy when the subproject is not part of a later build. mvn clean removes it again. Without an install or an earlier package, -pl core fails on Maven 4 as well.

title: Build several modules or leave one out
text: -pl takes a comma-separated list, -pl api,app . To build everything except some modules, put ! before them: mvn verify -pl '!app' The quotes keep shells such as
body: -pl takes a comma-separated list, -pl api,app . To build everything except some modules, put ! before them: mvn verify -pl '!app' The quotes keep shells such as Bash from treating ! as a history command. - works as well as ! : -pl -app . Maven 4: Selecting a subproject that is itself an aggregator selects its subprojects too, and excluding it excludes them. Maven 3 selects or excludes only the aggregator. Add -N ( --non-recursive ) on Maven 4 to select the aggregator alone.

page: Build part of a multi-module project
title: Resume a failed build
text: When a module fails, Maven skips the modules after it and prints where to pick up again: [ERROR] After correcting the problems, you can resume the build with th
terms: -rf core mvn verify -pl args -r --resume target resume.properties -fae -am Unrecognized option
body: When a module fails, Maven skips the modules after it and prints where to pick up again: [ERROR] After correcting the problems, you can resume the build with the command [ERROR] mvn <args> -rf :core Fix the problem and run the same command with -rf (resume from). Maven skips the modules that came before core in the build order: mvn verify -rf :core The modules before it are not rebuilt, so core takes them from the local repository, as with -pl . Maven 4: Maven 4 suggests mvn [args] -r instead. With -r ( --resume ), Maven reads the modules that failed or were skipped from target/resume.properties in the root directory, and builds only those. After -fae , that is the failed modules and their dependents, not everything that came after the first failure. Add -am to build the modules they need as well: mvn verify -r -am . Maven 3 does not know -r and stops with Unrecognized option: -r .

title: CI-friendly versions
text: Starting with Maven 3.5.0-beta-1 you can use the ${revision} , ${sha1} and/or ${changelist} as placeholders for the version in your pom file.
body: Starting with Maven 3.5.0-beta-1 you can use the ${revision} , ${sha1} and/or ${changelist} as placeholders for the version in your pom file.

title: Dependencies
text: A multi-module build often defines dependencies between modules. The usual way of defining dependencies and their versions has been to use ${project.version} an
body: A multi-module build often defines dependencies between modules. The usual way of defining dependencies and their versions has been to use ${project.version} and this has not been changed. So the correct way to do such things can be seen in the following example: <project> <modelVersion> 4.0.0 </modelVersion> <parent> <groupId> org.apache </groupId> <artifactId> apache </artifactId> <version> 18 </version> </parent> <groupId> org.apache.maven.ci </groupId> <artifactId> ci-parent </artifactId> <name> First CI Friendly </name> <version> ${revision} </version> ... <properties> <revision> 1.0.0-SNAPSHOT </revision> </properties> <modules> <module> child1 </module> .. </modules> </project> The child will look like this: <project> <modelVersion> 4.0.0 </modelVersion> <parent> <groupId> org.apache.maven.ci </groupId> <artifactId> ci-parent </artifactId> <version> ${revision} </version> </parent> <groupId> org.apache.maven.ci </groupId> <artifactId> ci-child </artifactId> ... <dependencies> <dependency> <groupId> org.apache.maven.ci </groupId> <artifactId> child2 </artifactId> <version> ${project.version} </version> </dependency> </dependencies> </project> If you try to use ${revision} instead of ${project.version} your build will fail.

title: Install / Deploy
text: To install or deploy artifacts by using the above setup, you have to use the Flatten Maven Plugin . Otherwise, you will install/deploy artifacts in the reposito
body: To install or deploy artifacts by using the above setup, you have to use the Flatten Maven Plugin . Otherwise, you will install/deploy artifacts in the repository which will not be consumable by Maven. Such a setup will look like this: <project> <modelVersion> 4.0.0 </modelVersion> <parent> <groupId> org.apache </groupId> <artifactId> apache </artifactId> <version> 18 </version> </parent> <groupId> org.apache.maven.ci </groupId> <artifactId> ci-parent </artifactId> <name> First CI Friendly </name> <version> ${revision} </version> ... <properties> <revision> 1.0.0-SNAPSHOT </revision> </properties> <build> <plugins> <plugin> <groupId> org.codehaus.mojo </groupId> <artifactId> flatten-maven-plugin </artifactId> <version> 1.1.0 </version> <configuration> <updatePomFile> true </updatePomFile> <flattenMode> resolveCiFriendliesOnly </flattenMode> </configuration> <executions> <execution> <id> flatten </id> <phase> process-resources </phase> <goals> <goal> flatten </goal> </goals> </execution> <execution> <id> flatten.clean </id> <phase> clean </phase> <goals> <goal> clean </goal> </goals> </execution> </executions> </plugin> </plugins> </build> <modules> <module> child1 </module> .. </modules> </project>

title: Multi-Subproject Setup (Maven 4)
text: When you are using Maven 4 with model version 4.1.0, you don't need to specify the versions of your subproject's parent and your project's own dependencies than
body: When you are using Maven 4 with model version 4.1.0, you don't need to specify the versions of your subproject's parent and your project's own dependencies thanks to automatic version resolution in Maven 4. In addition, you don't need the Flatten Maven Plugin like you did with Maven 3.

title: Multi-module Setup (Maven 3)
text: So now let us take a look into a situation where we have a multi-module build. We have a parent pom and one or more children. The parent pom will look like this
body: So now let us take a look into a situation where we have a multi-module build. We have a parent pom and one or more children. The parent pom will look like this: <project> <modelVersion> 4.0.0 </modelVersion> <parent> <groupId> org.apache </groupId> <artifactId> apache </artifactId> <version> 18 </version> </parent> <groupId> org.apache.maven.ci </groupId> <artifactId> ci-parent </artifactId> <name> First CI Friendly </name> <version> ${revision} </version> ... <properties> <revision> 1.0.0-SNAPSHOT </revision> </properties> <modules> <module> child1 </module> .. </modules> </project> The child will look like this: <project> <modelVersion> 4.0.0 </modelVersion> <parent> <groupId> org.apache.maven.ci </groupId> <artifactId> ci-parent </artifactId> <version> ${revision} </version> </parent> <groupId> org.apache.maven.ci </groupId> <artifactId> ci-child </artifactId> ... </project> A multi-module build builds the same way as the single project setup. You should define the version either via property in the parent or use the .mvn/maven.config file.

title: Single Project Setup
text: This can look like this: <project> <modelVersion> 4.0.0 </modelVersion> <parent> <groupId> org.apache </groupId> <artifactId> apache </artifactId> <version> 18
terms: revision mvn clean package Drevision SNAPSHOT maven.config sha1 changelist Dchangelist
body: This can look like this: <project> <modelVersion> 4.0.0 </modelVersion> <parent> <groupId> org.apache </groupId> <artifactId> apache </artifactId> <version> 18 </version> </parent> <groupId> org.apache.maven.ci </groupId> <artifactId> ci-parent </artifactId> <name> First CI Friendly </name> <version> ${revision} </version> ... </project> This is of course a simple situation where we use only ${revision} for brevity to show the general course. Based on the above pom you can build your project using: mvn clean package But wait there is a problem? Which version will the artifacts have? So you need to define the version for your artifacts. The first possibility is to use the command line like this: mvn -Drevision=1.0.0-SNAPSHOT clean package This will become cumbersome over the time. So the other solution for this is to simply use a property inside the pom file which looks like this: <project> <modelVersion> 4.0.0 </modelVersion> <parent> <groupId> org.apache </groupId> <artifactId> apache </artifactId> <version> 18 </version> </parent> <groupId> org.apache.maven.ci </groupId> <artifactId> ci-parent </artifactId> <name> First CI Friendly </name> <version> ${revision} </version> ... <properties> <revision> 1.0.0-SNAPSHOT </revision> </properties> </project> So now you can simply call Maven as usual like mvn clean package . You can of course change the version via the command line like this: mvn -Drevision=2.0.0-SNAPSHOT clean package Of course, you can use the .mvn/maven.config file for this. A note about the used properties. You can only use those named ${revision} , ${sha1} and/or ${changelist} and not other named properties like this: <project> <modelVersion> 4.0.0 </modelVersion> <parent> <groupId> org.apache </groupId> <artifactId> apache </artifactId> <version> 18 </version> </parent> <groupId> org.apache.maven.ci </groupId> <artifactId> ci-parent </artifactId> <name> First CI Friendly </name> <version> ${revision} </version> ... <properties> <revision> 1.0.0-${buildNumber}-SNAPSHOT </revision> </properties> </project> The above example will not work as expected . If you like to have more flexibility you can use a combination of the different properties like this: <project> <modelVersion> 4.0.0 </modelVersion> <parent> <groupId> org.apache </groupId> <artifactId> apache </artifactId> <version> 18 </version> </parent> <groupId> org.apache.maven.ci </groupId> <artifactId> ci-parent </artifactId> <name> First CI Friendly </name> <version> ${revision}${sha1}${changelist} </version> ... <properties> <revision> 1.3.1 </revision> <changelist> -SNAPSHOT </changelist> <sha1/> </properties> </project> If you like to make a version 2.0.0-SNAPSHOT this can simply being achieved by using this: mvn -Drevision=2.0.0 clean package Another usage example can be to make a release which can be done via (version 1.3.1): mvn -Dchangelist= clean package Or if you like to make a release with another version: mvn -Drevision=2.7.8 -Dchangelist= clean package Please read until the end of this documentation!

title: Modules in Maven 3
text: (If you're working with Maven 4, please refer to the Maven 4 edition of this guide ) As seen in the introduction to the POM, Maven supports project aggregation
body: (If you're working with Maven 4, please refer to the Maven 4 edition of this guide ) As seen in the introduction to the POM, Maven supports project aggregation in addition to project inheritance. This section outlines how Maven processes projects with multiple modules, and how you can work with them more effectively.

title: More information
text: Chapter 6. A Multi-module Project (Maven by Example)
body: Chapter 6. A Multi-module Project (Maven by Example)

title: The Reactor
text: The mechanism in Maven that handles multi-module projects is referred to as the reactor . This part of the Maven core does the following: Collects all the avail
body: The mechanism in Maven that handles multi-module projects is referred to as the reactor . This part of the Maven core does the following: Collects all the available modules to build Sorts the projects into the correct build order Builds the selected projects in order Reactor Sorting Because modules within a multi-module build can depend on each other, it is important that the reactor sorts all the projects in a way that guarantees any project is built before it is required. The following relationships are honoured when sorting projects: a project dependency on another module in the build a plugin declaration where the plugin is another module in the build a plugin dependency on another module in the build a build extension declaration on another module in the build the order declared in the <modules> element (if no other rule applies) Note that only "instantiated" references are used - dependencyManagement and pluginManagement elements do not cause a change to the reactor sort order. Command Line Options No special configuration is required to take advantage of the reactor, however it is possible to customize its behavior. The following command line switches are available: --resume-from - resumes a reactor from the specified project (e.g. when it fails in the middle) --also-make - build the specified projects, and any of their dependencies in the reactor --also-make-dependents - build the specified projects, and any that depend on them --fail-fast - the default behavior - whenever a module build fails, stop the overall build immediately --fail-at-end - if a particular module build fails, continue the rest of the reactor and report all failed modules at the end instead --non-recursive - do not use a reactor build, even if the current project declares modules and just build the project in the current directory Refer to the Maven command line interface reference for more information on these switches.

title: Reactor options
text: The command-line options that select, order and continue the modules of a multi-module build, the project selector syntax, and the Maven line each needs.
keywords: command line CLI flags project selector exclude module optional project parallel build threads resume.properties Could not find the selected project in the reactor The requested required projects do not exist Unrecognized option
body: These options change which modules of a multi-module build Maven builds, from where, and what happens when one fails. Without them, Maven builds the project in the current directory and all its modules. The complete list of command-line options is in the CLI options reference ; mvn --help prints it for the Maven you run. Build part of a multi-module project shows the common combinations.

title: Failures
text: Option Long form When a module fails Exit status Maven -ff --fail-fast Stops; all modules after it are skipped. The default. failure 3.9, 3.10, 4.0 -fae --fail-

body: Option Long form When a module fails Exit status Maven -ff --fail-fast Stops; all modules after it are skipped. The default. failure 3.9, 3.10, 4.0 -fae --fail-at-end Skips only the modules that depend on the failed one and builds the rest. failure 3.9, 3.10, 4.0 -fn --fail-never Builds all other modules, including those that depend on the failed one. success, although the log ends with BUILD FAILURE 3.9, 3.10, 4.0 With -fn , a module that depends on the failed module is built against whatever version of it Maven can find, such as an older one in the local repository. After a failure, Maven 3 prints the command to resume with, mvn <args> -rf :core . Maven 4 prints mvn [args] -r , and its target/resume.properties lists the failed and skipped modules. After a successful build, Maven 4 deletes that file.

text: Option Long form Effect Maven -T --threads Builds modules that do not depend on each other at the same time. Takes a thread count, -T 4 , or a count per CPU cor
body: Option Long form Effect Maven -T --threads Builds modules that do not depend on each other at the same time. Takes a thread count, -T 4 , or a count per CPU core with C , -T 1C . 3.9, 3.10, 4.0 The order of the modules still holds: a module starts only after the modules it depends on are finished. Maven logs Using the MultiThreadedBuilder implementation with a thread count of 4 .

title: Project selectors
text: -pl takes a comma-separated list of selectors, -rf takes one. Each selector names one module of the build. Selector Selects Example path the module in that dire
terms: -pl -rf core services billing artifactId groupId com.example.shop app -app docs Could not find the selected project in reactor The requested required projects do exist. shipping N
body: -pl takes a comma-separated list of selectors, -rf takes one. Each selector names one module of the build. Selector Selects Example path the module in that directory, relative to the current directory core , services/billing , ./core :artifactId the module with that artifact id :core groupId:artifactId the module with that group and artifact id com.example.shop:core A selector without a colon is always a path. When the directory name differs from the artifact id, the artifact id alone does not select the module: write it with a colon in front. Prefixes go before the selector: Prefix Meaning Example Maven ! or - exclude the module from the build -pl '!app' , -pl -app 3.9, 3.10, 4.0 + select the module; the same as no prefix -pl +core 3.9, 3.10, 4.0 ? do not fail when no module matches; goes after ! , - or + -pl '?docs' , -pl '!?docs' 4.0 Quote selectors with ! or ? in the shell: Bash treats ! as a history command and ? as a wildcard. A selector that matches no module stops the build before anything is built. Maven 3 reports Could not find the selected project in the reactor: docs , Maven 4 The requested required projects docs do not exist. Maven 3 reports ?docs the same way, as it does not know the ? prefix. Selecting or excluding an aggregator differs between the lines: Selector on an aggregator services with subprojects billing and shipping Maven 3.9, 3.10 Maven 4.0 -pl services services services , billing , shipping -pl services -N fails: -N leaves only the root project in the build services -pl '!services' everything except services everything except services , billing and shipping

title: Selecting modules
text: Option Long form Effect Maven -pl --projects Builds only the listed modules, a comma-separated list of project selectors . Modules they need come from the local

body: Option Long form Effect Maven -pl --projects Builds only the listed modules, a comma-separated list of project selectors . Modules they need come from the local repository unless they are selected too; Maven 4 looks in .mvn/target/project-local-repo first. 3.9, 3.10, 4.0 -am --also-make Adds the modules the selected ones depend on, directly or indirectly, and their parents. 3.9, 3.10, 4.0 -amd --also-make-dependents Adds the modules that depend on the selected ones, directly or indirectly. 3.9, 3.10, 4.0 -rf --resume-from Takes one project selector and leaves out every module that comes before it in the build order. 3.9, 3.10, 4.0 -r --resume Builds only the modules that failed or were skipped in the previous build, as recorded in target/resume.properties of the root directory. 4.0 -N --non-recursive Builds the POM in the current directory without its modules. With -pl on Maven 4: selects an aggregator without its subprojects. 3.9, 3.10, 4.0 -f --file Starts from another POM file, or the pom.xml in another directory, as if Maven ran there. 3.9, 3.10, 4.0 -am and -amd without -pl select nothing extra on Maven 3. On Maven 4 they apply to the project in the current directory, and reach the whole project even when you start in a subproject's directory. Maven 3 does not know -r and stops with Unrecognized option: -r . The CLI options reference describes the latest Maven 3 release; Maven 4 lists -r in mvn --help .

page: Share dependency versions and plugin configuration
title: Import a BOM
text: Many libraries publish a bill of materials (BOM): a POM that holds only a <dependencyManagement> section with the versions of all their artifacts that belong to
body: Many libraries publish a bill of materials (BOM): a POM that holds only a <dependencyManagement> section with the versions of all their artifacts that belong together. Import it into the parent's <dependencyManagement> with type pom and scope import : pom.xml <dependencyManagement> <dependencies> <dependency> <groupId> org.junit </groupId> <artifactId> junit-bom </artifactId> <version> 5.14.4 </version> <type> pom </type> <scope> import </scope> </dependency> </dependencies> </dependencyManagement> Modules then declare the artifacts of that library without a version: core/pom.xml <dependency> <groupId> org.junit.jupiter </groupId> <artifactId> junit-jupiter </artifactId> <scope> test </scope> </dependency> A version you write in <dependencyManagement> yourself wins over the version from an imported BOM. A POM has only one parent, but it can import any number of BOMs. The dependency mechanism describes the rules for imports in full.

page: Share dependency versions and plugin configuration
title: Lock plugin versions and configure plugins
text: <pluginManagement> does for plugins what <dependencyManagement> does for dependencies: it sets the version and configuration of a plugin without running it. The
body: <pluginManagement> does for plugins what <dependencyManagement> does for dependencies: it sets the version and configuration of a plugin without running it. The compiler, Surefire and the other plugins of the build lifecycle run in every jar module anyway, so for them the managed version and configuration take effect in every module. pom.xml <build> <pluginManagement> <plugins> <plugin> <groupId> org.apache.maven.plugins </groupId> <artifactId> maven-compiler-plugin </artifactId> <version> 3.16.0 </version> <configuration> <compilerArgs> <arg> -Xlint:all </arg> </compilerArgs> </configuration> </plugin> <plugin> <groupId> org.apache.maven.plugins </groupId> <artifactId> maven-surefire-plugin </artifactId> <version> 3.6.0 </version> </plugin> </plugins> </pluginManagement> </build> Without a version, each Maven release uses its own default for these plugins, so the same project builds with different plugin versions on different Maven versions. Maven 4: Maven 4 warns about every plugin of the lifecycle that has no version: Version not locked for default bindings plugins [maven-clean-plugin, maven-resources-plugin, maven-jar-plugin], you should define versions in pluginManagement section of your pom.xml or parent . Add those plugins to <pluginManagement> with a version to silence it.

page: Share dependency versions and plugin configuration
title: Manage dependency versions
text: <dependencyManagement> in the parent sets the version of a dependency without adding the dependency to any module. A module that needs it declares it without a
body: <dependencyManagement> in the parent sets the version of a dependency without adding the dependency to any module. A module that needs it declares it without a version and gets the managed one. List your own modules there as well, with ${project.version} , so that modules can depend on each other without a version. pom.xml <dependencyManagement> <dependencies> <dependency> <groupId> com.example.shop </groupId> <artifactId> api </artifactId> <version> ${project.version} </version> </dependency> <dependency> <groupId> com.example.shop </groupId> <artifactId> core </artifactId> <version> ${project.version} </version> </dependency> <dependency> <groupId> org.slf4j </groupId> <artifactId> slf4j-api </artifactId> <version> ${slf4j.version} </version> </dependency> </dependencies> </dependencyManagement> core/pom.xml <dependencies> <dependency> <groupId> com.example.shop </groupId> <artifactId> api </artifactId> </dependency> <dependency> <groupId> org.slf4j </groupId> <artifactId> slf4j-api </artifactId> </dependency> </dependencies> The managed version also applies when the library arrives as a transitive dependency of something else. A module that writes a <version> in its own dependency uses that version instead of the managed one. A dependency in the parent's <dependencies> , outside <dependencyManagement> , is added to every module. Keep that for what each module really needs.

page: Share dependency versions and plugin configuration
title: Run a plugin in some modules only
text: A plugin that is not part of the lifecycle runs only in modules that declare it. Put its version and executions in the parent's <pluginManagement> , here the so
terms: <pluginManagement> mvn verify api target api-1.0-SNAPSHOT-sources.jar core app <build> <plugins>
body: A plugin that is not part of the lifecycle runs only in modules that declare it. Put its version and executions in the parent's <pluginManagement> , here the source plugin that packages a jar with the sources: pom.xml <pluginManagement> <plugins> <plugin> <groupId> org.apache.maven.plugins </groupId> <artifactId> maven-source-plugin </artifactId> <version> 3.4.0 </version> <executions> <execution> <id> attach-sources </id> <goals> <goal> jar-no-fork </goal> </goals> </execution> </executions> </plugin> </plugins> </pluginManagement> Then declare it, without a version, in the modules that need it: api/pom.xml <build> <plugins> <plugin> <groupId> org.apache.maven.plugins </groupId> <artifactId> maven-source-plugin </artifactId> </plugin> </plugins> </build> mvn verify now creates api/target/api-1.0-SNAPSHOT-sources.jar , and no sources jar for core or app . To run a plugin in every module instead, declare it in the parent's <build><plugins> rather than in <pluginManagement> .

page: Share dependency versions and plugin configuration
title: Set a value once with a property
text: Properties defined in the parent are available in every module. Use them for settings that plugins read, and for version numbers you use in more than one place.
body: Properties defined in the parent are available in every module. Use them for settings that plugins read, and for version numbers you use in more than one place. pom.xml <properties> <maven.compiler.release> 17 </maven.compiler.release> <project.build.sourceEncoding> UTF-8 </project.build.sourceEncoding> <slf4j.version> 2.0.17 </slf4j.version> </properties> A module can override a property by defining it again in its own <properties> .

title: Split a project into modules
text: Turn one Maven project into a parent POM with modules that depend on each other and build together from the root directory.
keywords: multi-module multi-project monorepo submodule subproject parent POM aggregator reactor split jar restructure project
terms: <modules> <module> <subprojects> <parent> pom packaging ${project.version} .mvn shop api core app
body: Split a project into modules when parts of it should be built, tested or released as separate jars but still be built together. The steps below turn a project shop into three modules: api with interfaces, core that implements them, and app that uses core . The root POM becomes both the parent the modules inherit from and the aggregator that lists them; Aggregation and inheritance explains the two roles. The result has this layout: shop/ ├── pom.xml ├── api/ │ ├── pom.xml │ └── src/main/java/... ├── core/ │ ├── pom.xml │ └── src/main/java/... └── app/ ├── pom.xml └── src/main/java/...

title: Build from the root directory
text: Run Maven in the root directory: mvn verify Maven builds the parent and the modules in one run, in an order where every module comes after the modules it depend
terms: mvn verify target app app-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar core
body: Run Maven in the root directory: mvn verify Maven builds the parent and the modules in one run, in an order where every module comes after the modules it depends on. The summary at the end lists them in that order: [INFO] Reactor Summary for shop 1.0-SNAPSHOT: [INFO] [INFO] shop ............................................... SUCCESS [ 0.106 s] [INFO] api ................................................ SUCCESS [ 0.908 s] [INFO] core ............................................... SUCCESS [ 0.083 s] [INFO] app ................................................ SUCCESS [ 0.063 s] [INFO] ------------------------------------------------------------------------ [INFO] BUILD SUCCESS Each module's jar is in its own target directory, such as app/target/app-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar . Within this build, app uses the core built earlier in the same run; nothing has to be installed. To build only some of the modules, see Build part of a multi-module project .

title: Create a POM for each module
text: Each module gets a directory with the name you listed and a POM that names the root POM as its parent. The module inherits groupId and version , so it only decl
body: Each module gets a directory with the name you listed and a POM that names the root POM as its parent. The module inherits groupId and version , so it only declares its artifactId . api/pom.xml <project xmlns= "http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0" xmlns:xsi= "http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xsi:schemaLocation= "http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd" > <modelVersion> 4.0.0 </modelVersion> <parent> <groupId> com.example.shop </groupId> <artifactId> shop </artifactId> <version> 1.0-SNAPSHOT </version> </parent> <artifactId> api </artifactId> </project> The parent's POM is one directory up, where Maven looks first, so the <parent> needs no <relativePath> .

title: Make one module depend on another
text: A module uses another module through an ordinary dependency. Use ${project.version} as the version, so that the modules always use each other's current version.
body: A module uses another module through an ordinary dependency. Use ${project.version} as the version, so that the modules always use each other's current version. app/pom.xml <parent> <groupId> com.example.shop </groupId> <artifactId> shop </artifactId> <version> 1.0-SNAPSHOT </version> </parent> <artifactId> app </artifactId> <dependencies> <dependency> <groupId> com.example.shop </groupId> <artifactId> core </artifactId> <version> ${project.version} </version> </dependency> </dependencies> core depends on api in the same way. A module only sees the classes of the modules it depends on, directly or through another module.

title: Mark the root directory
text: Create an empty .mvn directory next to the root POM. Maven 3 accepts it, and Maven 4 uses it to find the root of the project; without it Maven 4 may warn Unable
terms: mvn Unable to find the root directory maven.config target gitignore mkdir
body: Create an empty .mvn directory next to the root POM. Maven 3 accepts it, and Maven 4 uses it to find the root of the project; without it Maven 4 may warn Unable to find the root directory . Git does not store empty directories, so add a file to it, for example an empty maven.config . Maven 4 writes build output to .mvn/target , so add that directory to your .gitignore . mkdir .mvn

title: Move the code into the modules
text: Every module has the standard directory layout of its own. Move the existing src directory into the module that gets most of the code, then move the other packa
body: Every module has the standard directory layout of its own. Move the existing src directory into the module that gets most of the code, then move the other packages to the other modules. With Git, git mv keeps the history of the files. In the root directory: mkdir core git mv src core/src The root directory now holds no sources, only the POM and the module directories.

title: Turn the root POM into a parent
text: Change the packaging of the root POM to pom , so that it builds no jar of its own, and list the module directories under <modules> . Keep the groupId , version
body: Change the packaging of the root POM to pom , so that it builds no jar of its own, and list the module directories under <modules> . Keep the groupId , version and properties: the modules inherit them. pom.xml <project xmlns= "http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0" xmlns:xsi= "http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xsi:schemaLocation= "http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd" > <modelVersion> 4.0.0 </modelVersion> <groupId> com.example.shop </groupId> <artifactId> shop </artifactId> <version> 1.0-SNAPSHOT </version> <packaging> pom </packaging> <modules> <module> api </module> <module> core </module> <module> app </module> </modules> <properties> <maven.compiler.release> 17 </maven.compiler.release> <project.build.sourceEncoding> UTF-8 </project.build.sourceEncoding> </properties> </project> Move the project's <dependencies> out of the root POM into the modules that use them. Dependencies left in the parent are added to every module. To keep their versions in one place, see Share dependency versions and plugin configuration .

title: Use subprojects on Maven 4
text: Maven 4: With model version 4.1.0 the root POM lists <subprojects> instead of <modules> , or lists nothing at all: a pom -packaged 4.1.0 POM without either elem
terms: <subprojects> <modules> pom pom.xml <parent Unrecognised tag subprojects app core
body: Maven 4: With model version 4.1.0 the root POM lists <subprojects> instead of <modules> , or lists nothing at all: a pom -packaged 4.1.0 POM without either element builds every direct subdirectory that has a pom.xml . A subproject can name its parent with an empty <parent/> , which means the POM one directory up, and can depend on another subproject without a version. Maven 3 cannot read these POMs; it stops with Unrecognised tag: 'subprojects' . pom.xml <project xmlns= "http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.1.0" xmlns:xsi= "http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xsi:schemaLocation= "http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.1.0 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.1.0.xsd" > <modelVersion> 4.1.0 </modelVersion> <groupId> com.example.shop </groupId> <artifactId> shop </artifactId> <version> 1.0-SNAPSHOT </version> <packaging> pom </packaging> <subprojects> <subproject> api </subproject> <subproject> core </subproject> <subproject> app </subproject> </subprojects> </project> app/pom.xml <project xmlns= "http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.1.0" xmlns:xsi= "http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xsi:schemaLocation= "http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.1.0 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.1.0.xsd" > <modelVersion> 4.1.0 </modelVersion> <parent/> <artifactId> app </artifactId> <dependencies> <dependency> <groupId> com.example.shop </groupId> <artifactId> core </artifactId> </dependency> </dependencies> </project> When it installs or deploys app , Maven 4 writes the parent's coordinates and the version of core into the published POM, so projects built with Maven 3 can use it.

title: Subprojects in Maven 4
text: (If you're working with Maven 3, please refer to the Maven 3 edition of this guide ) As seen in the introduction to the POM, Maven supports project aggregation
body: (If you're working with Maven 3, please refer to the Maven 3 edition of this guide ) As seen in the introduction to the POM, Maven supports project aggregation in addition to project inheritance. This section outlines how Maven processes projects with multiple subprojects, and how you can work with them more effectively.

title: Command Line Options
text: No special configuration is required to take advantage of the reactor, however it is possible to customize its behavior. The following command line switches are
body: No special configuration is required to take advantage of the reactor, however it is possible to customize its behavior. The following command line switches are available: Long Short Summary Details --file -f Selects an alternative POM file or directory containing a POM file. Collecting subprojects --non-recursive -N Ignores any child subprojects that may be present in the starting POM. When combined with -pl , ignores the children of selected subprojects. Collecting subprojects and Relationships between subprojects --projects -pl Specifies the subprojects to include or exclude from a build. Inclusion and exclusion --also-make -am Builds the specified subprojects, and any of their dependencies in the reactor. Relationships between subprojects --also-make-dependents -amd Builds the specified subprojects, and any that depend on them. Relationships between subprojects --resume-from -rf Resumes a reactor from the specified project (e.g. when it fails in the middle). Dealing with failures --resume -r Resumes a reactor from the subproject where the previous build failed. Dealing with failures --fail-fast -ff Stops the overall build immediately whenever a subproject build fails. This is the default behavior. Dealing with failures --fail-at-end -fae Continues the rest of the reactor if a particular subproject build fails and report all failed subprojects at the end instead. Dealing with failures --fail-never -fn Never fails the build, regardless of the project result. Dealing with failures
